\DocumentMetadata{tagging=off}

%\let\batchmode\relax

\documentclass{l3in2edoc}

\let\subsubsubsection\paragraph

\usepackage{xcolor,csquotes,alltt}
\usepackage{todonotes}
% [pass]: keep the l3doc layout; only used for \newgeometry in the index
\usepackage[pass]{geometry}

% l3doc (like ltxdoc) sets this to "File" for the source listings
\renewcommand\partname{Part}

\ExplSyntaxOn \makeatletter
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_names_parse_one_aux:nnNn #1#2#3#4
  {
    \bool_if:NTF #3
      {
        \tl_if_head_eq_charcode:nNTF {#2} :
          { \__codedoc_names_parse_aux:nnn {#4} {#4} { \scan_stop: } }
          {
            \exp_args:Ne \__codedoc_names_parse_aux:nnn
              { \__codedoc_base_form_aux:nnN {#1} {#2} #3 }
              {#1} {#2}
          }
      }
      {
%        \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_macro_TF_bool
%          { \msg_error:nne { l3doc } { no-signature-TF } {#4} }
        \__codedoc_names_parse_aux:nnn {#4} {#4} { \scan_stop: }
      }
  }


% Next lines make "int" acceptable in the optional arg to function but
% it doesn't do much yet. How should internal functions be marked?
% For now I simply marked the commands in red as in (don't use or rely
% on).

\keys_define:nn { l3doc/function }
  {
    int .value_forbidden:n = true ,
    int .code:n =
      {
        \bool_set_true:N \l__codedoc_macro_internal_bool
      } ,
    readonly .value_forbidden:n = true ,
    readonly .code:n =
      {
        \bool_set_true:N \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
      } ,
    settable .value_forbidden:n = true ,   % only used by update-usage.py
    settable .code:n = { } ,
    user .value_forbidden:n = true ,
    user .code:n =
      {
        \bool_set_true:N \l__codedoc_macro_user_bool
      } ,
  }

\bool_new:N \l__codedoc_macro_user_bool

% Source file(s) of an entry, shown in the right margin next to the
% entry heading. The \sourcefile lines directly before each entry are
% generated by interface2-usage/update-usage.py from the current kernel
% sources (definitions may move between releases). To suppress the
% notes, e.g., for printing, use
%    \RenewDocumentCommand \SourceFileNote {m} {}
\tl_new:N \g__interfacetwo_source_tl
\NewDocumentCommand \sourcefile { m }
  { \tl_gset:Nn \g__interfacetwo_source_tl {#1} }
\NewDocumentCommand \SourceFileNote { m }
  {
    \rlap
      {
        \hskip \textwidth \hskip \marginparsep
        \parbox [t] { 5em }
          {
            \raggedright \scriptsize \ttfamily
            \clist_use:nn {#1} { \\ }
          }
      }
  }
% The tagging code follows latex-lab-testphase-l3doc, which redefines
% this command (and \__codedoc_typeset_functions:) as well; without it the
% structures opened and closed elsewhere don't match.
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_function_typeset_start:
  {
    \par \bigskip
    \UseTaggingSocket{struct/begin}{tag=\UseStructureName{doc/function}}
    \cs_if_exist_use:N \tagpdfparaOff
    \noindent
    % the margin note is an artifact; with tagging stopped it creates no
    % structure (the names must stay the first child, the Caption)
    \tl_if_empty:NF \g__interfacetwo_source_tl
      {
        \tag_mc_begin:n { artifact }
        \tag_stop:
        \exp_args:NV \SourceFileNote \g__interfacetwo_source_tl
        \tag_start:
        \tag_mc_end:
        \tl_gclear:N \g__interfacetwo_source_tl
      }
  }

% Constants: data that is set up by the kernel (possibly in several
% steps, e.g., code added to a kernel hook during the format build)
% but must not be changed outside the kernel. Typeset like variables.
% Constants and read-only variables show "(constant)", "(constants)"
% or "(read-only)" instead of a syntax example.
\bool_new:N \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
\seq_new:N \l__interfacetwo_names_seq
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_marker:n #1
  {
    \begin{syntax}
      \normalfont \emph { (#1) }
    \end{syntax}
  }
\DeclareDocumentEnvironment { constant } { O{} +v }
  {
    \__codedoc_function:nnw {#1} {#2}
    \seq_set_split:Nnn \l__interfacetwo_names_seq { , } {#2}
    \seq_remove_all:Nn \l__interfacetwo_names_seq { }
    \__interfacetwo_marker:n
      {
        constant
        \int_compare:nNnT { \seq_count:N \l__interfacetwo_names_seq } > 1 { s }
      }
  }
  { \__codedoc_function_end: }
% Variables: the option "readonly" marks state that only the kernel
% should change.
\DeclareDocumentEnvironment { variable } { O{} +v }
  {
    \bool_set_false:N \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
    \__codedoc_function:nnw {#1} {#2}
    \bool_if:NT \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
      { \__interfacetwo_marker:n { read-only } }
  }
  { \__codedoc_function_end: }

\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_typeset_functions:
  {
    \small\ttfamily
    \__codedoc_target:
    \Hy@MakeCurrentHref { HD. \int_use:N \c@HD@hypercount }
    \__codedoc_date_compare:VNVF \l__codedoc_date_added_tl > \l__codedoc_base_date_tl
      { \tl_clear:N \l__codedoc_date_added_tl }
    \__codedoc_date_compare:VNVF \l__codedoc_date_updated_tl > \l__codedoc_base_date_tl
      { \tl_clear:N \l__codedoc_date_updated_tl }
    \group_begin:
      \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_macro_internal_bool { \color{red}  }
      \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_macro_user_bool     { \color{blue} }
      \UseTaggingSocket{struct-mc}{tag=\UseStructureName{doc/functionnames}}
        {
          \cs_if_exist:NT \tagpdfsetup
            { \tagpdfsetup{table/tagging=div} }
          \AssignStructureRole{table/row}{\UseStructureName{doc/functionname}}
          \AssignStructureRole{table/cell}{\UseStructureName{doc/functionnamepart}}
          \begin{tabular} [t] { @{} l @{} >{\hspace{\tabcolsep}} r @{} }
            \toprule
            \__codedoc_function_extra_labels:
            \__codedoc_names_typeset:
            \__codedoc_typeset_dates:
            \bottomrule
          \end{tabular}
        }
    \group_end:
    \normalfont\normalsize\par
  }

% Arrow for "expands to/results in" in examples. A text glyph (TU
% U+2192, TS1 fallback) rather than math, so it also works inside alltt
% and doesn't produce a math structure when tagging.
\NewDocumentCommand \textyields {} { \textrightarrow }

% Usage of commands outside the core (sweep over TeX Live
% texmf-dist/tex/latex). These lines are generated by
% interface2-usage/update-usage.py -- don't edit them by hand; put
% corrections into interface2-usage/config.toml and rerun the script.
% They are placed directly after \end{function} or
% \end{variable} (not inside) so that long lists can break across
% pages. The optional argument names the command (without backslash)
% when an entry documents several commands.
%
%  \modifiedby    packages that redefine or patch a command (or set a
%                 constant); always printed in full as this shouldn't
%                 happen
%  \setby         packages that set a variable meant to be set (e.g.,
%                 \@currentlabel or \topsep), or redefine a function
%                 meant to be redefined
%  \usedby        packages that only use an internal ("int") command
%  \publicusedby  packages that use a command that is fine to use;
%                 separate so that these lists can easily be dropped
%
% The source always records the complete list; \setby, \usedby and
% \publicusedby print at most \UsageListMax names followed by the
% total. An empty list (command checked, no usage found) prints
% nothing.

\int_new:N \l__interfacetwo_max_int
\int_new:N \l__interfacetwo_count_int
\clist_new:N \l__interfacetwo_clist
\NewDocumentCommand \UsageListMax { m }
  { \int_set:Nn \l__interfacetwo_max_int {#1} }
\UsageListMax { 20 }

% The packages in "Modified by" lists are shown in red; to turn that
% off use \RenewDocumentCommand \ModifiedByFormat {} {}
\NewDocumentCommand \ModifiedByFormat {} { \color{red} }

\NewDocumentCommand \modifiedby { o m }
  {
    \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Modified } { modified } {#1} {#2}
      \c_false_bool { \ModifiedByFormat }
  }
% For deprecated entries the packages in the "Set by" and "Used by"
% lists are shown in red as well (they still use something that should
% go away); to turn that off use
% \RenewDocumentCommand \DeprecatedUsageFormat {} {}
\NewDocumentCommand \DeprecatedUsageFormat {} { \color{red} }
% set at the end of each entry (the option is local to the environment)
\bool_new:N \g__interfacetwo_deprecated_bool
\cs_new:Npn \__interfacetwo_deprecated_format:
  { \bool_if:NT \g__interfacetwo_deprecated_bool { \DeprecatedUsageFormat } }

\NewDocumentCommand \setby { o m }
  {
    \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Set } { set } {#1} {#2} \c_true_bool
      { \__interfacetwo_deprecated_format: }
  }
\NewDocumentCommand \usedby { o m }
  {
    \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Used } { used } {#1} {#2} \c_true_bool
      { \__interfacetwo_deprecated_format: }
  }
\NewDocumentCommand \publicusedby { o m }
  {
    \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Used } { used } {#1} {#2} \c_true_bool
      { \__interfacetwo_deprecated_format: }
  }

% #6: formatting applied to the package list only
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn #1#2#3#4#5#6
  {
    \clist_set:Nn \l__interfacetwo_clist {#4}
    \clist_if_empty:NF \l__interfacetwo_clist
      {
        \par \addvspace { \smallskipamount }
        { \footnotesize \raggedright \noindent
          \textbf
            {
              \tl_if_novalue:nTF {#3}
                { #1 \c_space_tl by: }
                { \cs[no-index]{#3} \c_space_tl #2 \c_space_tl by: }
            } ~
          #6
          \bool_lazy_and:nnTF {#5}
            {
              \int_compare_p:nNn
                { \clist_count:N \l__interfacetwo_clist } > \l__interfacetwo_max_int
            }
            {
              \int_zero:N \l__interfacetwo_count_int
              \clist_map_inline:Nn \l__interfacetwo_clist
                {
                  \int_incr:N \l__interfacetwo_count_int
                  \int_compare:nNnTF \l__interfacetwo_count_int > \l__interfacetwo_max_int
                    { \clist_map_break: }
                    { \int_compare:nNnF \l__interfacetwo_count_int = 1 { , ~ } ##1 }
                }
              \c_space_tl \ldots \c_space_tl (total~of~ \clist_count:N \l__interfacetwo_clist
                \c_space_tl packages)
            }
            { \clist_use:Nn \l__interfacetwo_clist { , ~ } }
          \par
        }
      }
  }

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
% Index
%
% l3doc is set up for expl3 code: names containing @ (but no _ or :)
% are collected under "TeX and LaTeX2e commands" as subitems, and all
% pages are typeset the same (italic "usage"). For interface2 we want
% a plain alphabetical index:
%
% - no module grouping; names are sorted as written (so names starting
%   with @ come under "Symbols");
% - the page with the description (function, variable or constant
%   environment) is bold, pages that only mention the command are
%   upright;
% - \IndexingOff / \IndexingOn suppress index entries in between (used
%   for the example commands like \foo in the Conventions section).

\cs_new_eq:NN \__interfacetwo_key_get_orig:n \__codedoc_key_get:n
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_key_get:n #1
  {
    \__interfacetwo_key_get_orig:n {#1}
    \str_if_eq:VnT \l__codedoc_index_module_tl { TeX }
      {
        \tl_clear:N \l__codedoc_index_module_tl
      }
    % \ , \, and \_ end up with an empty key, which makeindex rejects
    % (the first two because l3doc's name parsing loses the space and
    % the comma; see interface2-issues.md)
    \tl_if_blank:VT \l__codedoc_index_key_tl
      { \tl_set_eq:NN \l__codedoc_index_key_tl \c_backslash_str }
  }

% Index entries of the commands described by a function, variable or
% constant environment are written by the heading (before the body is
% typeset) and recorded in \g__interfacetwo_index_described_seq. Mentions
% of these commands inside the body of the same environment (syntax
% line, description) are not indexed, so the page doesn't appear twice
% (bold and upright; makeindex would also warn about conflicting
% encaps). The list is cleared when the environment starts and ends.
\bool_new:N \l__interfacetwo_index_described_bool
\bool_new:N \g__interfacetwo_index_bool
\bool_gset_true:N \g__interfacetwo_index_bool
\seq_new:N \g__interfacetwo_index_described_seq
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_function_index:n #1
  {
    \__codedoc_if_macro_internal:nF {#1}
      { \seq_gput_right:Nn \g_doc_functions_seq {#1} }
    \bool_set_true:N \l__interfacetwo_index_described_bool
    \__codedoc_special_index:nn {#1} { usage }
    \bool_set_false:N \l__interfacetwo_index_described_bool
  }
\cs_new_eq:NN \__interfacetwo_function_init_orig: \__codedoc_function_init:
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_function_init:
  {
    \seq_gclear:N \g__interfacetwo_index_described_seq
    \__interfacetwo_function_init_orig:
  }
\cs_new_eq:NN \__interfacetwo_function_end_orig: \__codedoc_function_end:
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_function_end:
  {
    \bool_gset_eq:NN \g__interfacetwo_deprecated_bool
      \l__codedoc_macro_deprecated_bool
    \__interfacetwo_function_end_orig:
    \seq_gclear:N \g__interfacetwo_index_described_seq
  }
% Plain page numbers: l3doc writes "MMMMI-<page>" to sort page entries
% before code-line entries, which interface2 doesn't have; with the
% source2e.ist page_precedence makeindex then sorts such pages wrongly.
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_index_page_orig:nn #1#2
  {
    \protected@write \@indexfile { }
      { \string \indexentry { #1 \encapchar hdpindex{#2} } { \thepage } }
  }
% the write is not immediate, so the encap has to be chosen now
% #1 refers to l3doc's variables (\l__codedoc_index_escaped_key_tl, ...)
% and can contain markup (\meta, ...), so for storing and comparing we
% use the key and the printed form as strings, without expanding them.
\tl_new:N \l__interfacetwo_index_entry_tl
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_index_page_hc:nn #1#2
  {
    \bool_if:NT \g__interfacetwo_index_bool
      {
        \__interfacetwo_index_meta:
        \tl_set:Ne \l__interfacetwo_index_entry_tl
          {
            \tl_to_str:N \l__codedoc_index_escaped_key_tl =
            \tl_to_str:N \l__codedoc_index_escaped_macro_tl
          }
        \bool_if:NTF \l__interfacetwo_index_described_bool
          {
            \seq_gput_right:NV \g__interfacetwo_index_described_seq
              \l__interfacetwo_index_entry_tl
            \__interfacetwo_index_page_orig:nn {#1} { IndexDescribed }
            \__interfacetwo_index_record:
          }
          {
            \seq_if_in:NVF \g__interfacetwo_index_described_seq
              \l__interfacetwo_index_entry_tl
              { \__interfacetwo_index_mention:nn {#1} {#2} }
          }
      }
  }
% A mention outside the environment can still fall on the page where
% the command is described. To catch that, the described entry records
% its page in the .aux file (at shipout, when the page is known), and in
% the next run a mention on a recorded page writes nothing. The test is
% done at shipout as well, hence the \exp_not:N's; the entry is passed
% to \use_none:n or \use:n, so no conditional tokens inside it are ever
% skipped.
\tl_new:N \l__interfacetwo_index_hash_tl
\cs_new_protected:Npn \InterfaceTwoDescribed #1#2
  { \cs_gset_eq:cN { interfacetwo@described@ #1 @ #2 } \scan_stop: }
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_index_record:
  {
    \tl_set:Ne \l__interfacetwo_index_hash_tl
      { \str_mdfive_hash:e { \l__interfacetwo_index_entry_tl } }
    \protected@write \@auxout { }
      {
        \string \InterfaceTwoDescribed { \l__interfacetwo_index_hash_tl }
          { \thepage }
      }
  }
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_index_mention:nn #1#2
  {
    \tl_set:Ne \l__interfacetwo_index_hash_tl
      { \str_mdfive_hash:e { \l__interfacetwo_index_entry_tl } }
    \protected@write \@indexfile { }
      {
        \exp_not:N \ifcsname
          interfacetwo@described@ \l__interfacetwo_index_hash_tl @ \thepage
        \exp_not:N \endcsname
          \exp_not:N \expandafter \exp_not:N \use_none:n
        \exp_not:N \else
          \exp_not:N \expandafter \exp_not:N \use:n
        \exp_not:N \fi
        { \string \indexentry { #1 \encapchar hdpindex{#2} } { \thepage } }
      }
  }
% Environment names: \env{name} prints the name and makes two index
% entries, "name (environment)" at the top level and "name" under
% "Environments". Not in the table of contents (l3doc switches indexing
% off there) and not where \IndexingOff is active.
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_index_env:n #1
  {
    \bool_lazy_and:nnT
      { \g__interfacetwo_index_bool } { \l__codedoc_allow_indexing_bool }
      {
        \protected@write \@indexfile { }
          {
            \string \indexentry
              {
                #1 \actualchar \string \texttt {#1} \space (environment)
                \encapchar hdpindex{usage}
              }
              { \thepage }
          }
        \protected@write \@indexfile { }
          {
            \string \indexentry
              {
                Environments \levelchar #1 \actualchar \string \texttt {#1}
                \encapchar hdpindex{usage}
              }
              { \thepage }
          }
      }
  }
\RenewDocumentCommand \env { m } { \texttt {#1} \__interfacetwo_index_env:n {#1} }
\AtBeginDocument
  { \cs_if_exist:NT \pdfstringdefDisableCommands
      { \pdfstringdefDisableCommands { \def \env #1 {#1} } } }

\NewDocumentCommand \IndexingOff { } { \bool_gset_false:N \g__interfacetwo_index_bool }
\NewDocumentCommand \IndexingOn  { } { \bool_gset_true:N  \g__interfacetwo_index_bool }

% page formats used by the index entries (via hdpindex)
\cs_gset_protected:Npn \IndexDescribed #1 { \textbf {#1} }
\cs_gset_protected:Npn \usage #1 {#1}

\IndexPrologue
  {
    \part*{Index}
    \markboth{Index}{Index}
    \addcontentsline{toc}{part}{Index}
    Bold~numbers~denote~the~page~where~the~
    command~is~described,~all~others~indicate~pages~where~it~is~mentioned.
  }

% Placeholders in command names (concept entries such as
% \the\meta{counter}): l3doc prints the names of function/variable
% entries verbatim, and \cs{the\meta{counter}} is indexed with the
% tokenized \meta in the key (see interface2-issues.md). So both the
% entry heading and the argument of \cs are processed as strings:
% \meta{x} in them is typeset as \meta{x}, the index key keeps the
% string "\meta{x}" (so mentions and the description share one index
% entry) and the index shows \meta{x} as well. A backslash that is part
% of the name in front of a placeholder is written \\meta{x}, e.g.
% \cs{\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd}} for the encoding-specific commands.
\tl_new:N \l__interfacetwo_meta_tl
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_meta_typeset:n #1
  {
    \tl_set:Nn \l__interfacetwo_meta_tl {#1}
    \regex_replace_all:nnN
      { \\meta \ * \{ ( [^\{\}]* (?: \{ [^\{\}]* \} [^\{\}]* )* ) \} }
      { \c{__interfacetwo_meta_rescan:n} \cB\{ \1 \cE\} }
      \l__interfacetwo_meta_tl
    \l__interfacetwo_meta_tl
  }
\cs_generate_variant:Nn \__interfacetwo_meta_typeset:n { V }
% the argument of \meta is a string here; rescan it, so that, e.g.,
% \meta{mathversion\textsubscript{1}} works
\tl_new:N \l__interfacetwo_meta_arg_tl
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_meta_rescan:n #1
  {
    % (\cs has already replaced the spaces by \@xobeysp)
    \tl_set:Nn \l__interfacetwo_meta_arg_tl {#1}
    \tl_replace_all:Nnn \l__interfacetwo_meta_arg_tl { \@xobeysp } { ~ }
    \exp_args:NNnV \tl_set_rescan:Nnn \l__interfacetwo_meta_arg_tl { }
      \l__interfacetwo_meta_arg_tl
    \exp_args:NV \meta \l__interfacetwo_meta_arg_tl
  }
% copy of l3doc's version, printing the name with \__interfacetwo_meta_typeset:n
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_typeset_function_block:nN #1#2
  {
    \__codedoc_function_index:e
      { #1 \bool_if:NT #2 { \tl_to_str:n {TF} } }
    \__codedoc_function_label:eN {#1} #2
    \__interfacetwo_meta_typeset:n {#1}
    \bool_if:NT #2 { \__codedoc_typeset_TF: }
    \__codedoc_typeset_expandability:
    \seq_if_empty:NF \g__codedoc_variants_seq
      { \__codedoc_typeset_variant_list:nN {#1} #2 }
    \\
  }
% copy of l3doc's \__codedoc_cmd:nn (behind \cs), same change
\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_cmd:nn #1#2
  {
    \bool_set_false:N \l__codedoc_cmd_noindex_bool
    \bool_set_true:N \l__codedoc_cmd_replace_bool
    \tl_set:Nn \l__codedoc_cmd_index_tl { \q_no_value }
    \tl_set:Nn \l__codedoc_cmd_module_tl { \q_no_value }
    \keys_set:nn { l3doc/cmd } {#1}
    \tl_set:Nn \l__codedoc_cmd_tl {#2}
    % a name with placeholders (\cs{the\meta{counter}}, also
    % \cs{?\\meta{cmd}} where \\ is a control symbol followed by the
    % letters "meta") is processed as a string, written as in an entry
    % heading (no space after \meta)
    \exp_args:NnV \regex_match:nnT { \c{meta} | \c{\\} meta \{ }
      \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
      {
        \tl_set:Ne \l__codedoc_cmd_tl { \tl_to_str:N \l__codedoc_cmd_tl }
        \regex_replace_all:nnN { (\\meta) \ + (\{) } { \1 \2 }
          \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
      }
    \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_cmd_replace_bool
      {
        \tl_set_rescan:Nnn \l__codedoc_tmpb_tl { } { _ }
        \tl_replace_all:NVn \l__codedoc_cmd_tl \l__codedoc_tmpb_tl { _ }
        \__codedoc_replace_at_at:N \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
        \tl_replace_all:NnV \l__codedoc_cmd_tl { _ } \l__codedoc_tmpb_tl
      }
    \mode_if_math:T { \mbox }
      {
        \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_allow_indexing_bool { \__codedoc_target: }
        \verbatim@font
        \__codedoc_if_almost_str:VT \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
          {
            \__kernel_tl_set:Nx \l__codedoc_cmd_tl { \tl_to_str:N \l__codedoc_cmd_tl }
            \bool_if:NT \g__codedoc_cs_break_bool
              {
                \regex_replace_all:nnN
                  { ([^\\\_]\_*) \_ ([^\_]) }
                  { \1 \c{BreakableUnderscore} \2 }
                  \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
              }
          }
        \tl_replace_all:Nnn \l__codedoc_cmd_tl { ~ } { \@xobeysp }
        \__interfacetwo_meta_typeset:V \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
        \@
      }
    \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_allow_indexing_bool
      {
        \bool_if:NF \l__codedoc_cmd_noindex_bool
          {
            \quark_if_no_value:NF \l__codedoc_cmd_index_tl
              {
                \__kernel_tl_set:Nx \l__codedoc_cmd_tl
                  { \c_backslash_str \exp_not:o { \l__codedoc_cmd_index_tl } }
              }
            \exp_args:No \__codedoc_key_get:n { \l__codedoc_cmd_tl }
            \quark_if_no_value:NF \l__codedoc_cmd_module_tl
              {
                \__kernel_tl_set:Nx \l__codedoc_index_module_tl
                  { \tl_to_str:N \l__codedoc_cmd_module_tl }
              }
            \__codedoc_special_index_module:ooonN
              { \l__codedoc_index_key_tl }
              { \l__codedoc_index_macro_tl }
              { \l__codedoc_index_module_tl }
              { usage }
              \l__codedoc_index_internal_bool
          }
      }
  }
% in the index: the escaped name gives \verb*&...!\meta{x}...& (each
% backslash written as \quotechar\tl_to_str:N\bslash); show \meta{x} by
% ending \verb* around it
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_index_meta:
  {
    \regex_replace_all:nnN
      {
        \c{quotechar} \c{tl_to_str:N} \c{bslash} meta
        \{ ( [^\{\}]* (?: \{ [^\{\}]* \} [^\{\}]* )* ) \}
      }
      { \& \c{string} \c{meta} \cB\{ \1 \cE\} \c{string} \c{verb} \* \& }
      \l__codedoc_index_escaped_macro_tl
  }

\date{Released 2026-09-16}

\pagenumbering{roman}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
  I spent a bit of a rainy afternoon making a list of all \LaTeXe{}
  commands in the kernel as input for something like
  the \texttt{cmdguide} or as a reference manual
  named \texttt{interface2}.

  So far this only covers commands from \texttt{latex.ltx}. Those from
  related files would need adding too.

  By now a good number of entries got classified and documented. The
  documentation was written with support from Claude, which speeds up
  the process considerably (even though checking and correcting was/is
  an important task). But overall this starts to look like something
  useful.

  Frank
\end{abstract}


\tableofcontents

\part{Introduction}

\section{Conventions}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \foo, \foovariant
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{foo} \oarg{optional arg} \Arg{mandatory arg}
  \end{syntax}
  General form of documentation for commands. Commands that share a
  common behavior/interface may be documented together like this.

  The syntax box gives one example with arguments. Commands that are
  not user-level and take no arguments (variables, constants,
  internal helpers) have no syntax box.
  Data that may change is documented as a variable; a variable that
  only the kernel should change is marked \emph{(read-only)}. Data
  that is set up by the kernel (possibly in several steps) and never
  changes afterwards is documented as a constant. A command that is not yet
  documented has no explanation afterwards.

  After an entry, lists of packages in \TeX\,Live give the usage of
  its commands outside the core: \enquote{Modified by} lists packages
  that redefine or patch a command, which normally shouldn't happen
  (always shown in full); \enquote{Set by} lists packages that set a
  variable that is meant to be set (such as \cs{@currentlabel} or
  \cs{topsep}) or redefine a function that is meant to be redefined
  (such as the \cs{...@elt} markers of data lists); \enquote{Used by} lists
  packages that only use a
  command (not given for user commands). Long \enquote{Set by} and
  \enquote{Used by} lists show only the first names and the total.
  The lists come from an automated search of \texttt{tex/latex} that
  excludes the core bundles, so they are indicative only.

\end{function}
\modifiedby[foovariant]{}
\publicusedby[foovariant]{}

\begin{function}[TF]
  {
    \foo
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fooF} \Arg{text arg} \Arg{false branch}
  \end{syntax}
  Conditionals using the \texttt{TF} convention are documented like
  this.  In \LaTeXe{} commands normally do not indicate the arguments
  they take (\texttt{TF} is one of the exceptions). But any other
  arguments aren't indicated so one has to \enquote{know}.

  In contrast,
  commands from the L3 programming layer always denote their argument
  signature in the name (via the \texttt{:} convention).
  
\end{function}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \foo
  }
  Internal commands that should not be relied on are marked in red.
  
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \foo
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{foo} 
  \end{syntax}
  %
  Document-level (user) commands are shown in blue. In addition
  commands that are mainly for class and package writer but can also
  be useful in the document preamble or inside the document are also
  marked this way. This means that basically all core commands
  documented in \emph{The LaTeX{} Companion}\cite{tlc3} are shown in
  blue.
  
\end{function}

\begin{function}[EXP]
  {
    \foo
  }
  Fully expandable functions, i.e., those that can be used
  inside \cs{edef} or \cs{expanded} are indicated with a star.

  Most user commands can be safely put into \cs{edef} but then do
  nothing at all (because they are internally protected either
  by \cs{protect} or by being defined with \cs{protected}). Such
  commands are not marked with a star!
  
\end{function}

%===============================================
\section{Defining commands and environments}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Document commands with extended syntax}

\sourcefile{ltcmd}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \NewDocumentCommand,
    \RenewDocumentCommand,
    \DeclareDocumentCommand,
    \ProvideDocumentCommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewDocumentCommand} \meta{cmd} \Arg{arg spec} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} as a robust document command whose arguments are
  described by \meta{arg spec}, e.g., \texttt{m} for a mandatory
  argument, \texttt{o} or \texttt{O\Arg{default}} for an optional
  argument in brackets, \texttt{s} for a star, and so on. Inside
  \meta{code} the arguments are available as \texttt{\#1},
  \texttt{\#2}, etc. The variants differ only in what happens if
  \meta{cmd} is already defined (or not): \cs[no-index]{New\ldots}
  gives an error if it exists, \cs[no-index]{Renew\ldots} gives an
  error if it doesn't, \cs[no-index]{Provide\ldots} silently does
  nothing if it exists, and \cs[no-index]{Declare\ldots} always
  defines it.
  This is the recommended interface for new commands that take
  arguments; for details see \texttt{usrguide}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[NewDocumentCommand]{}
\modifiedby[RenewDocumentCommand]{}
\modifiedby[DeclareDocumentCommand]{}
\modifiedby[ProvideDocumentCommand]{}



\sourcefile{ltcmd}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \NewExpandableDocumentCommand,
    \RenewExpandableDocumentCommand,
    \DeclareExpandableDocumentCommand,
    \ProvideExpandableDocumentCommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewExpandableDocumentCommand} \meta{cmd} \Arg{arg spec} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{NewDocumentCommand} and friends, but \meta{cmd} is made
  expandable, so it can be used inside \cs{edef}, \cs{csname}, or
  similar contexts. In return the \meta{arg spec} is restricted: the
  last argument must be mandatory and some types (such as
  verbatim arguments) are not supported. Only use this if expandability
  is really needed.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[NewExpandableDocumentCommand]{}
\modifiedby[RenewExpandableDocumentCommand]{}
\modifiedby[DeclareExpandableDocumentCommand]{}
\modifiedby[ProvideExpandableDocumentCommand]{}

\subsection{Argument specifiers, processors and tests}

\sourcefile{ltcmd}
\begin{function}[TF,user]
  {
    \IfBoolean
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{IfBooleanTF} \meta{boolean} \Arg{true} \Arg{false}
  \end{syntax}
  Tests if \meta{boolean} is either \cs{BooleanFalse} or
  \cs{BooleanTrue} and selects the corresponding argument for further
  processing.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\begin{constant}

    \BooleanFalse,
    \BooleanTrue

  \texttt{s} and \texttt{t} (star or token present or not). They
  should only be tested with \cs{IfBooleanTF}, never by comparing them
  directly.
\end{constant}

\sourcefile{ltcmd}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \SplitArgument
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    >\{\cs{SplitArgument} \Arg{number} \Arg{token}\} m
  \end{syntax}
  Argument processor that splits the argument at each \meta{token}
  into exactly \meta{number}${}+1$ parts, which are passed on as
  separate brace groups (missing parts become \cs{NoValue}). Too many
  occurrences of \meta{token} produce an error.
\end{function}

\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltcmd}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ProcessList
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    >\{\cs{SplitList} \Arg{token}\} m
    \cs{ProcessList} \Arg{list} \Arg{function}
  \end{syntax}
  The argument processor \cs{SplitList} turns an argument into a list
  of items separated by \meta{token}. \cs{ProcessList} then applies
  \meta{function} to each item, passing the item as an argument.
\end{function}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Classic command definitions}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newcommand,
    \renewcommand,
    \providecommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcommand} * \meta{cmd} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} to take \meta{num} arguments (0--9, default 0),
  referred to as \texttt{\#1}, \ldots, \texttt{\#9} in \meta{code}. If
  \meta{default} is given, the first argument becomes optional (in
  brackets) and \meta{default} is used when it is absent; all further
  arguments are mandatory. \cs{newcommand} gives an error if
  \meta{cmd} is already defined, \cs{renewcommand} if it isn't, and
  \cs{providecommand} makes the definition only if \meta{cmd} is
  undefined.

  Without the star the arguments are \cs{long}, i.e., may contain
  \cs{par}; the starred form produces commands whose arguments can't.
  Commands without arguments are never made \cs{long} (since 2025/11).
  For more complex argument structures use \cs{NewDocumentCommand}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[newcommand]{autoarea, beamerbaseoverlay, colonequals,
  combine, opcit, pdfx, standalone}
\modifiedby[renewcommand]{algorithm2e, beamerbaseoverlay, scrbase,
  scrbase-20260202}
\modifiedby[providecommand]{revtex4-1, revtex4-2, vncaps.tex}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \\\meta{cmd}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{\\meta{cmd}}
  \end{syntax}
  The inner command of a command \cs{\meta{cmd}} defined with
  \cs{newcommand} (or \cs{renewcommand}, \cs{providecommand}) with an
  optional argument: its name is a backslash followed by the name of
  \cs{\meta{cmd}}; it takes all arguments with the optional one delimited
  by brackets, while \cs{\meta{cmd}} supplies the default. The name contains
  characters other than letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Environments}

\sourcefile{ltcmd}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \NewDocumentEnvironment,
    \RenewDocumentEnvironment,
    \DeclareDocumentEnvironment
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewDocumentEnvironment} \Arg{name} \Arg{arg spec} \Arg{begin code} \Arg{end code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines the environment \meta{name} with arguments described by
  \meta{arg spec}, as for \cs{NewDocumentCommand}. The arguments are
  available in both \meta{begin code} and \meta{end code}. A
  \texttt{b} in the \meta{arg spec} grabs the whole environment body
  as an argument. The variants differ in their handling of existing
  definitions, as for the corresponding command declarations
  (\cs{ProvideDocumentEnvironment} also exists).
\end{function}
\modifiedby[NewDocumentEnvironment]{}
\modifiedby[RenewDocumentEnvironment]{}
\modifiedby[DeclareDocumentEnvironment]{}



\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newenvironment,
    \renewenvironment
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newenvironment} * \Arg{name} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{begin code} \Arg{end code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines the environment \meta{name}; arguments are handled as for
  \cs{newcommand} but are only available in \meta{begin code}. To use
  them in \meta{end code} they have to be saved first (or use
  \cs{NewDocumentEnvironment}). The environment is implemented by the
  commands \cs[no-index]{\meta{name}} and \cs[no-index]{end\meta{name}}, so
  \cs{newenvironment} fails if either already exists.
  \cs{renewenvironment} gives an error if the environment is undefined.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[newenvironment]{beamerbaseoverlay, combine, gmdoc}
\modifiedby[renewenvironment]{beamerbaseoverlay}

  \end{syntax}
  The workhorse behind \cs{renewenvironment} after the star has been
  processed. Use \cs{renewenvironment} instead.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltmiscen}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \begin,
    \end
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{name}\meta{argument(s)} ... \cs{end}\Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Start and end the environment \meta{name}. \cs{begin} opens a
  group, executes the environment hooks and \cs[no-index]{\meta{name}}
  (which picks up the arguments); \cs{end} executes
  \cs[no-index]{end\meta{name}}, checks that \meta{name} matches the
  innermost open environment (otherwise an error is given), and
  closes the group. Hence all local settings inside an environment
  are undone at its end.

  This is not the engine primitive \cs{end} but a \LaTeX{} command replacing
  it; the original primitive is still available as \cs{@@end}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[int]
  {

  }

    \cs{@currenvline}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \\meta{env},
    \end\meta{env}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{\meta{env}} \meta{arguments of the environment, if any}
    \cs{end\meta{env}} \quad \% no arguments
  \end{syntax}
  The begin and end code of the environment \meta{env}:
  \cs{begin}\Arg{env} executes \cs{\meta{env}} and \cs{end}\Arg{env}
  \cs{end\meta{env}}. Defined by \cs{newenvironment} etc. (for
  environments defined with \cs{NewDocumentEnvironment} these are
  internal helpers). Many environments are documented here by these two
  commands, e.g., \cs{itemize} and \cs{enditemize}. \meta{env} may
  contain characters other than letters; then the commands can only be
  used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse},
  \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}

\subsection{Copying, showing and comparing definitions}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \CheckCommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{CheckCommand} * \meta{cmd} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Takes the same arguments as \cs{newcommand} but defines nothing.
  Instead, it checks that \meta{cmd} currently has exactly that
  definition and issues a warning if not. Default values for optional
  arguments are not compared. Useful in packages before redefining a
  kernel or package command, to detect that some other package has
  already changed it. Only usable in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{neoschool, pxeverysel}

  dateiliste, dvipscol, everysel-2011-10-28, fix-tudscrfonts, fncylab,

    \check@command,

\sourcefile{ltdefns}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \\meta{cmd}\meta{space}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{\meta{cmd}\meta{space}}
  \end{syntax}
  The inner command of a robust command \cs{\meta{cmd}} defined with
  \cs{DeclareRobustCommand}: its name is that of \cs{\meta{cmd}} followed by
  a space, and it holds the actual definition, while \cs{\meta{cmd}} only
  calls \cs{protect}\cs{\meta{cmd}\meta{space}}. Commands made robust with
  \cs{MakeRobust} use the same scheme. The name contains characters other
  than letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}

\subsection{Parsing arguments by hand}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@ifnextchar
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@ifnextchar} \meta{char} \Arg{true} \Arg{false}
  \end{syntax}
  Looks at the next non-space token in the input: if it is
  (\cs{ifx}-equal to) \meta{char}, \meta{true} is executed, otherwise
  \meta{false}. The token itself is not removed. Spaces in front of it
  are skipped (and lost). Typically used to test for an optional
  argument with \texttt{[}.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@dblarg
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@dblarg} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Calls \meta{cmd}, which must take an optional and a mandatory
  argument, such that if the optional argument is missing, the
  mandatory argument is used for it too. E.g., \cs{section} uses it
  so that the heading text is also the default for the table of
  contents entry.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@testopt
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@testopt} \meta{cmd} \Arg{default}
  \end{syntax}
  If the next token is \texttt{[}, calls \meta{cmd}; otherwise calls
  \meta{cmd}\texttt{[}\meta{default}\texttt{]}. Implements commands
  whose first argument is optional, e.g.,
  \cs{def}\cs[no-index]{foo}\texttt{\{}\cs{@testopt}\cs[no-index]{@foo}\texttt{\{default\}\}}.
\end{function}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Low-level definitions}

These are \TeX{} primitives; they are listed here because package
code uses them all the time. Unlike \cs{newcommand} they never check
whether the command already exists.



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \def
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{def} \meta{cmd} \meta{parameter text} \Arg{replacement text}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} locally. The \meta{parameter text} consists of
  parameters \texttt{\#1} to \texttt{\#9} (in order), possibly mixed
  with delimiter tokens; e.g., with \texttt{\#1.\#2} as \meta{parameter
  text} the first argument is delimited by a dot. Prefixes \cs{global},
  \cs{long}, and \cs{protected} can
  be put in front. The \meta{replacement text} is stored unexpanded.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{hyperref, pdfnotiz, srdp-tables, tabu}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \edef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{edef} \meta{cmd} \meta{parameter text} \Arg{replacement text}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{def}, but the \meta{replacement text} is fully expanded at
  definition time. Robust \LaTeX{} commands survive this unchanged, but
  fragile ones may break; if the text can contain arbitrary user input
  use \cs{protected@edef} instead.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

  {
    \xdef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{xdef} \meta{cmd} \meta{parameter text} \Arg{replacement text}
  \end{syntax}
  Same as \cs{global}\cs{edef}. The \LaTeX{} variant that respects
  \cs{protect} is \cs{protected@xdef}. (There is also the primitive
  \cs{gdef}, the same as \cs{global}\cs{def}.)

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \let
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{let} \meta{cmd} \texttt{=} \meta{token}
  \end{syntax}
  Gives \meta{cmd} the current meaning of \meta{token} (the
  \texttt{=} and one following space are optional). If \meta{token} is
  a macro, \meta{cmd} becomes a copy of it that does not change if
  \meta{token} is later redefined. Note that this doesn't work properly
  for robust commands defined with \cs{DeclareRobustCommand} or with
  an optional argument via \cs{newcommand}; use \cs{NewCommandCopy}
  for them.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \futurelet
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{futurelet} \meta{cmd} \meta{token\textsubscript1} \meta{token\textsubscript2}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets \meta{cmd} to the meaning of \meta{token\textsubscript2} (\`a
  la \cs{let}) and then executes \meta{token\textsubscript1} with
  \meta{token\textsubscript2} still in the input. This is the basis
  for look-ahead commands like \cs{@ifnextchar}, which should normally be
  used instead.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@namedef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@namedef}\Arg{name}\meta{parameter text}\Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Equivalent to \cs{def}\cs[no-index]{\meta{name}}\meta{parameter
  text}\Arg{code}, but the command name is given as a string, which is
  expanded inside \cs{csname}, e.g.,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{@namedef}\{ver@\#1.sty\}\{\meta{date and version}\}
  \end{alltt}
  No check is made whether the command already exists. The definition
  is local.

\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[EXP]
  {
    \@nameuse
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@nameuse}\Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Expands to the command \cs[no-index]{\meta{name}}. If that command is
  undefined it gets the meaning \cs{relax} as a side effect of
  \cs{csname} (so it then counts as defined for \cs{ifdefined} but
  not for \cs{@ifundefined}) and no error is raised.

\end{function}

\subsection{Internals of the definition commands}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@star@or@long
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@star@or@long} \meta{definer}
  \end{syntax}
  Looks ahead for a star, sets \cs{l@ngrel@x} accordingly, resets
  \cs{pr@tectedrel@x} to \cs{relax}, and then calls \meta{definer}
  (e.g., \cs{new@command}). This is how \cs{newcommand} and friends
  implement their star forms.

\end{function}

  catoptions, cnltx-base, combine, elsarticle, etoolbox, exp-testopt,

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \l@ngrel@x,
    \pr@tectedrel@x
  }
  Either \cs{relax} or \cs{long} (respectively \cs{protected}); inserted in
  front of the \cs{def} that \cs{newcommand} and friends finally
  execute. Their values are only meaningful inside the definition
  machinery, so don't set or test them elsewhere.

\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@ifdefinable
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@ifdefinable} \meta{cmd} \Arg{code}

  \cs{newcommand} and \cs{newlength}.
\end{function}

  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@car} \meta{item\textsubscript1} \meta{items} \cs{@nil}
    \cs{@cdr} \meta{item\textsubscript1} \meta{items} \cs{@nil}
    \cs{@carcube} \meta{item\textsubscript1} \meta{item\textsubscript2} \meta{item\textsubscript3} \meta{items} \cs{@nil}
  \end{syntax}
  List operations (named after their Lisp counterparts) on the
  material up to \cs{@nil}, where an \meta{item} is a single token or
  a brace group. \cs{@car} returns \meta{item\textsubscript1} (with
  braces removed) and drops the rest, \cs{@cdr} drops
  \meta{item\textsubscript1} and returns the remaining \meta{items},
  and \cs{@carcube} returns the first three items (with braces
  removed) and drops the rest. For example,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{@car} abc\cs{@nil} \textyields{} a
    \cs{@cdr} abc\cs{@nil} \textyields{} bc
  \end{alltt}
  The material must contain at least one item (\cs{@carcube}: four).
  \cs{@car} and \cs{@cdr} are not \cs{long}, so the material must not
  contain \cs{par}.

\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@gobble,
    \@gobbletwo,
    \@gobblethree,
    \@gobblefour
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@gobble} \Arg{arg}
    \cs{@gobblefour}\Arg{arg\textsubscript{1}}\Arg{arg\textsubscript{2}}\Arg{arg\textsubscript{3}}\Arg{arg\textsubscript{4}}
  \end{syntax}
  Remove one to four arguments (each a single token or a brace
  group) from the input. They are \cs{long}, so the arguments may
  contain \cs{par}. Typically used as the branch of a conditional that
  should do nothing, or to remove unwanted tokens.
\end{function}

\subsection{Conditionals and tests}

\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \ifnot@nil
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ifnot@nil} \Arg{test code} \Arg{true code}
  \end{syntax}
  If \meta{test code} is not the token \cs{@nnil} (compared via a
  scratch macro with \cs{ifx}), executes \meta{true code}, otherwise
  removes it. Despite its name it tests for \cs{@nnil} and not
  \cs{@nil}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{ltxkeys, ltxtools-doc, ltxtools-trace, xwatermark}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \TextOrMath
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{TextOrMath} \Arg{text code} \Arg{math code}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes \meta{text code} outside math mode and \meta{math code}
  inside. Unlike a test with \cs{ifmmode} it works correctly at the
  start of an alignment cell. Typically used for symbols available in
  text and math.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{aastex701, footmisc-2011-06-06, footmisx, hyperref, lwarp,
  textalpha, zugferd}



\sourcefile{ltfssdcl}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \in@
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{in@} \Arg{in-tokens} \Arg{tokens}
  \end{syntax}
  Tests if \meta{in-tokens} are inside \meta{tokens} and sets
  \cs{ifin@} to true or false accordingly. (The L3 programming layer
  has much better conditionals for this.)
\end{function}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Loops}

For new code the L3 programming layer offers much better loop
constructs (e.g., \texttt{\textbackslash clist\_map\_inline:nn}); the
loops below are mostly of interest for reading existing code.



\sourcefile{ltcntrl}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@whilenum
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@whilenum} \meta{\TeX{} boolean expression} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  \meta{\TeX{} boolean expression} is an expression that can follow
  after \cs{ifnum}, e.g., \cs{@tempcnta}\texttt{>5}. While the
  condition is true \meta{loop body} is executed which is supposed to
  alter the condition eventually, e.g., by changing \cs{@tempcnta} in
  this example. The loop is not executed in a group.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltcntrl}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@for
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@for} \meta{cmd} := \meta{comma list} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes \meta{loop body} for each item of \meta{comma list}, with
  \meta{cmd} defined (locally, via \cs{def}) to the current item. The
  \meta{comma list} is expanded once, so it can be a macro holding the
  list. Spaces around items are not removed and empty items are
  processed. Afterwards the loop variable is \cs{ifx}-equal to \cs{@nnil}.

  Does not work in code where \cs{ExplSyntaxOn} is active because
  there \texttt{:} has a different \cs{catcode}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{pronunciation, xfor}

\sourcefile{ltcntrl}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@tfor
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@tfor} \meta{cmd} := \meta{tokens} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  Loops over all items in \meta{tokens} (single tokens or brace groups;
  spaces are skipped) and defines \meta{cmd} to contain the next
  item and then processes the \meta{loop body} until it runs out of
  items or \cs{@break@tfor} is seen in the \meta{loop body}. Unlike
  \cs{@for}, the \meta{tokens} are not expanded.

  The L3 programming layer has much better functions for such
  programming tasks!
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@break@tfor
  }
%
  Can be used in the \meta{loop body} of \cs{@tfor} to end the loop
  before running out of tokens. It has to be used at the top level of
  the loop body (not inside a conditional of its own), as it removes
  the remaining loop code and closes the loop's conditionals.
\end{function}

\subsection{Lists and token manipulation}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@cons
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@cons} \meta{list cmd} \Arg{item}
  \end{syntax}
  Appends \cs{@elt}\,\meta{item} globally to \meta{list cmd}. The
  \meta{item} is expanded with \cs{edef} (except for \cs{@elt}), so
  it normally should be a single command or protected material. Lists
  of this form, e.g., \cs{cl@\meta{counter}}, are processed by locally
  defining \cs{@elt} and then executing the \meta{list cmd}.

\end{function}
\modifiedby{locality, scrlayer}

  bigfoot, caption3, caption3\_2010-01-14, caption3\_2011-11-01,

  changebar, cuted, dblfloatfix, dcounter, endfloat, eqparbox,
  fewerfloatpages, fix2col, fmultico, hyperref, hyperxmp,
  latex-xetex-bidi.def, llncs, ltxgrid, manyfoot, marginfix, memoir,
  mftinc, morefloats, newfloat, newfloat\_v1.0, newfloat\_v1.1,
  nidanfloat, paracol, paracol-2018-12-31, refart, refrep, revtex4,

\sourcefile{ltclass}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \zap@space
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{zap@space} \meta{material} \verb*/ /\cs{@empty}
  \end{syntax}
  Removes all spaces (at the top level, i.e., not inside braces) from
  \meta{material}. It grabs everything up to the first space, returns
  it and drops the space. Then it checks if the token after the space
  was \cs{@empty}. If yes, it stops processing, otherwise it
  recursively calls itself on the rest of \meta{material}. Usually
  used inside an \cs{edef}, e.g., to clean up a comma separated list.

  For this to work the \meta{material} is not allowed to contain
  \verb*/ /\cs{@empty}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\subsection{Character codes and category codes}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \makeatletter,
    \makeatother
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{makeatletter} \meta{material} \cs{makeatother}
  \end{syntax}
  Set the catcode of the \texttt{@}-sign to \enquote{letter}
  (respectively back to \enquote{other}) so that internal \LaTeXe{}
  commands can be accessed, e.g., in the document preamble. Not
  needed in package and class files where \texttt{@} is a letter
  anyway. Note that catcodes are fixed when text is read, so this
  doesn't work inside an argument of another command.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[makeatletter]{arabtex.tex, bussproofs, chess, poemscol,
  skdoc}
\modifiedby[makeatother]{arabtex.tex, at, bussproofs, poemscol, tvz-hax}



\sourcefile{latexrelease}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ExplSyntaxOn,
    \ExplSyntaxOff
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ExplSyntaxOn} ... \cs{ExplSyntaxOff}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets up the programming conventions for the L3 programming layer,
  e.g., spaces are ignored and \texttt{\_} and \texttt{:} are letters
  so can be used in command names; \texttt{\textasciitilde} produces
  a space. (The \texttt{@}-sign is not altered.)
\end{function}
\modifiedby[ExplSyntaxOn]{chextras}
\modifiedby[ExplSyntaxOff]{chextras}



\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@sanitize
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begingroup}\cs{@sanitize} \ldots{} \cs{endgroup}
  \end{syntax}
  Changes the catcodes of all special characters (space,
  \texttt{\textbackslash}, \texttt{\$}, \texttt{\&}, \texttt{\#},
  \texttt{\textasciicircum}, \texttt{\_}, \texttt{\%},
  \texttt{\textasciitilde}) to \enquote{other} (12), but not those of
  braces. Used, e.g., for reading arguments of \cs{index} and
  \cs{glossary} verbatim. The change is local, so it should be used
  inside a group.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{amsldoc, at, fancyvrb, gmverb, gmverse, listings,
  sanitize-umlaut, syntax, xdoc2}

\sourcefile{ltdirchk}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \dospecials
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{def}\cs{do}\#1\{\ldots\}    \cs{dospecials}
  \end{syntax}
  \cs{dospecials} calls \cs{do} for a list of typical \LaTeX{} syntax
  characters so that with an appropriate definition of \cs{do}
  something can be done for each of them, typically
  \cs{let}\cs{do}\cs{@makeother} to set up verbatim reading. The list is:
  \verb=\  \\ \{ \} \$ \& \# \^ \_ \% \~ \^^I=
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newcatcodetable
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcatcodetable} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Lua\TeX{} only: allocates a new catcode table and defines
  \meta{cmd} as its number, for use with \cs{catcodetable},
  \cs{initcatcodetable}, and \cs{savecatcodetable}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{collargs, hyperxmp, ucharcat}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{constant}
  {
    \catcodetable@initex,
    \catcodetable@string,
    \catcodetable@latex,
    \catcodetable@atletter
  }
  Lua\TeX{} only: predefined catcode tables for the Ini\TeX{}
  settings, for \enquote{string} catcodes (everything other, space a
  space), for the standard \LaTeX{} document settings, and for those
  with \texttt{@} as a letter. Useful, e.g., with \cs{scantextokens}
  or in Lua's \texttt{tex.print}.
\end{constant}
\modifiedby[catcodetable@initex]{}
\modifiedby[catcodetable@string]{}
\modifiedby[catcodetable@latex]{}
\modifiedby[catcodetable@atletter]{}

\publicusedby[catcodetable@string]{}
\publicusedby[catcodetable@latex]{}
\publicusedby[catcodetable@atletter]{chinesecal, collargs}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \setrangecatcode
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setrangecatcode} \Arg{first} \Arg{last} \Arg{catcode}
  \end{syntax}
  Lua\TeX{} only: sets the catcode of all characters with codes
  \meta{first} to \meta{last} to \meta{catcode}.
\end{function}

\publicusedby{}

\begin{constant}
  {
    \@percentchar
  }
  Expands to a percent character with category code 12 (other). Use it
  to write a \texttt{\%} into a file or into the log, e.g., with
  \cs{immediate}\cs{write} or \cs{typeout}, where \cs{\%} would not
  work.
\end{constant}

\sourcefile{ltcntrl}
\begin{constant}
  {
    \@nnil
  }
%
  Macro that serves as a delimiter in constructions with delimited
  arguments and as an end marker in lists, e.g.,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{@defaultunits}\cs{@tempdimb} \#5pt\cs{relax}\cs{@nnil}
  \end{alltt}
  It expands to the undefined \cs{@nil}, so it must never be
  executed; loops such as \cs{@for} compare an item with it using
  \cs{ifx} to detect the end (see also \cs{ifnot@nil}). \cs{@nil}
  itself is used only as an argument delimiter.
\end{constant}

\begin{constant}
  {
    \@empty
  }
%
  A macro that expands to nothing. Can be used, for example, to test
  with \cs{ifx} if a macro replacement text is empty. The definition
  is not \cs{long} which is an important restriction in such tests: a
  \cs{long} macro with empty replacement text is not \cs{ifx}-equal to
  \cs{@empty}.
\end{constant}

\begin{constant}

    \@depth,
    \@height,
    \@minus,
    \@plus,
    \@width
  }
  Macros holding the keywords \texttt{depth}, \texttt{height},
  \texttt{minus}, \texttt{plus}, and \texttt{width}, e.g., for use in
  \cs{hrule}\cs{@height}\texttt{2pt}. They date from the time when
  memory was scarce and storing a command used fewer tokens.
\end{constant}

\subsection{Scratch registers and macros}

Scratch registers may be changed by any kernel or package command, so
their value is only reliable between commands you control. They
should only be set locally.



\sourcefile{ltfinal,ltdirchk,ltspace}
\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \reserved@a,
    \reserved@b,
    \reserved@c,
    \reserved@d,
    \reserved@e,
    \reserved@f
  }

  Internal scratch commands used by the kernel. They should not be
  used in package code.
\end{variable}

%===============================================
\section{Registers and allocation}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Allocating registers}

The allocation commands below allocate registers globally. Use
\cs{newcounter} and \cs{newlength} for document-level counters and
lengths.



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newcount,
    \newdimen,
    \newskip,
    \newmuskip,
    \newtoks
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcount} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  A new integer (count), dimen, skip, muskip, or toks register is
  allocated and the command \meta{cmd} refers to it. No check is made
  whether \meta{cmd} is already defined (unlike \cs{newlength}). All
  registers available in the engine (normally 32768 or more) can be
  allocated.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[newcount]{bussproofs, etex}
\modifiedby[newdimen]{bussproofs, etex}
\modifiedby[newskip]{bussproofs, etex}
\modifiedby[newmuskip]{etex}
\modifiedby[newtoks]{etex}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newinsert
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newinsert} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Allocates a new insertion class (which uses box, count, dimen, and
  skip registers of the same number) and defines \meta{cmd} as its
  number. Inserts are used, e.g., for footnotes and floats.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \chardef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{chardef} \meta{cmd} \texttt{=} \meta{number}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} to typeset character
  \meta{number}. Since \meta{cmd} can also be used where \TeX{}
  expects a number, it is often used to define integer constants
  (0--255, or larger in Unicode engines), e.g., \cs{@xxxii}.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

\subsection{Allocation internals}

\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \insc@unt,
    \allocationnumber
  }
  Internal counters to manage \TeX{} registers: the last insert
  number allocated (inserts are allocated downwards) and the number of
  the most recently allocated register.
\end{variable}
\modifiedby[insc@unt]{}
\modifiedby[allocationnumber]{}
\usedby[insc@unt]{bussproofs, bytefield, etex, nath, pinlabel, seminar,
  tvz-code}
\usedby[allocationnumber]{bytefield, elocalloc, etex, fspdefault.tex,
  fspolddefault.tex, inputnormalization, latexbangla-engine-luatex.tex,
  luacolor, morewrites, oz, program, regstats, shadethm}



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \alloc@
  }
  The plain \TeX{} interface for allocating registers, now implemented
  with \cs{e@alloc}. Use the \cs{new...} commands instead.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{etex}
\usedby{bussproofs, minitoc, pinlabel, seminar, tvz-code,
  unicode-persianmath}



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \e@alloc
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{e@alloc} \meta{type} \meta{definer} \meta{counter} \meta{reserved} \meta{max} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Generic register allocator: increments \meta{counter}, checks it
  against \meta{max} with \cs{e@ch@ck}, and defines \meta{cmd} with
  \meta{definer} (e.g., \cs{countdef}) as the next register of
  \meta{type}. Used by all \cs{new...} register commands.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{bigfoot, bytefield, elocalloc, gloss-czech.ldf,
  gloss-polish.ldf, gloss-slovak.ldf, mathfam256, mathtools, morefloats,
  msu-thesis, songs}



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{constant}[int]
  {
    \e@alloc@top
  }
  The highest register number available in the current engine
  (e.g., 32767 or 65535).
\end{constant}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{elocalloc}



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \e@ch@ck
  }
  Helper for \cs{e@alloc} that checks if the register limit is
  reached, skipping register numbers reserved for inserts and
  giving an error if no register is left.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{bytefield, elocalloc}



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{constant}[int]
  {
    \e@insert@top
  }
  The highest register number that can be used for an insertion class
  (255 in engines with a limited number of inserts).
\end{constant}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{}

\subsection{Manipulating registers}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@defaultunits
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@defaultunits} \meta{register} \meta{value} pt\cs{relax}\cs{@nnil}
  \end{syntax}
  The \meta{register} which can be a dimen or skip register is
  assigned the \meta{value}, which can be a dimen or an integer
  value. In the latter case the integer is interpreted as a number of
  \texttt{pt}s.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[EXP]
  {
    \strip@pt
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{strip@pt} \meta{dimen register}
  \end{syntax}
  Expands to the value of \meta{dimen register} in points without the
  unit, e.g., \texttt{12} or \texttt{0.5}. The argument can be any
  internal dimen that can follow \cs{the}, e.g., \cs{dimexpr}
  \meta{expression}\cs{relax}. Often used to compute font sizes or
  scale factors.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \advance,
    \divide
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{advance} \meta{register} \texttt{by} \meta{value}
  \end{syntax}

  Change the register value by adding or
  dividing (integer division, truncating). The \texttt{by} is
  optional. The change is local unless prefixed by \cs{global}. There
  is also \cs{multiply}. For more complex calculations \cs{numexpr}
  or \cs{dimexpr} are usually easier.

  These are engine primitives.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[advance]{}
\modifiedby[divide]{}

\subsection{Lua\TeX{} and Xe\TeX{} specific allocation}

\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newattribute
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newattribute} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Allocates a new attribute register (Lua\TeX{} only) and defines
  \meta{cmd} as an \cs{attributedef} referring to it. Attributes
  are attached to nodes and can be inspected in Lua code.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{gloss-korean.ldf}
\publicusedby{babelbidi-fontfallback.def, gloss-chinese.ldf,
  gloss-japanese.ldf, gloss-tibetan.ldf, latexbangla-engine-luatex.tex,
  luacolor}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \setattribute,
    \unsetattribute
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setattribute} \meta{attribute} \Arg{value}
    \cs{unsetattribute} \meta{attribute}
  \end{syntax}
  Lua\TeX{} only: set the attribute register \meta{attribute}
  (allocated with \cs{newattribute}) to \meta{value} (an integer
  expression), or mark it as unset. The assignment is local.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[setattribute]{}
\modifiedby[unsetattribute]{gloss-korean.ldf}
\publicusedby[setattribute]{luacolor}
\publicusedby[unsetattribute]{gloss-chinese.ldf, gloss-japanese.ldf,
  hangulmath}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newluafunction
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newluafunction} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Lua\TeX{} only: allocates an index in the Lua function table
  (\texttt{lua.get\_functions\_table()}) and defines \meta{cmd} as
  that number. The Lua function is then called with
  \cs{luafunction}\meta{cmd}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{inputnormalization, letterspace, mathfont}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newluacmd,
    \newprotectedluacmd
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newluacmd} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Lua\TeX{} only: like \cs{newluafunction}, but defines \meta{cmd}
  via \cs{luadef} so that using \meta{cmd} directly calls the Lua
  function stored at its index. The \texttt{protected} variant makes
  \meta{cmd} \cs{protected}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[newluacmd]{}
\modifiedby[newprotectedluacmd]{}
\publicusedby[newluacmd]{}
\publicusedby[newprotectedluacmd]{}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newwhatsit,
    \newluabytecode,
    \newluachunkname
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newwhatsit} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Lua\TeX{} only: allocate a number for a user-defined whatsit node,
  a Lua bytecode register, or a Lua chunk name and define \meta{cmd}
  as that number. \cs{newluachunkname} also registers the name of
  \meta{cmd} as the name of the chunk (shown in Lua error messages).
\end{function}
\modifiedby[newwhatsit]{}
\modifiedby[newluabytecode]{}
\modifiedby[newluachunkname]{}
\publicusedby[newwhatsit]{}
\publicusedby[newluabytecode]{}
\publicusedby[newluachunkname]{}



\sourcefile{ltluatex}
\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \e@alloc@attribute@count,
    \e@alloc@whatsit@count
  }
  Counters holding the last allocated attribute and whatsit numbers.
\end{variable}
\modifiedby[e@alloc@attribute@count]{}
\modifiedby[e@alloc@whatsit@count]{}
\usedby[e@alloc@attribute@count]{}
\usedby[e@alloc@whatsit@count]{}



\sourcefile{ltfinal}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newXeTeXintercharclass
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newXeTeXintercharclass} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Xe\TeX{} only: allocates a new inter-character class for the
  \cs{XeTeXinterchartoks} mechanism and defines \meta{cmd} as its
  number.
\end{function}

%===============================================
\section{Counters and lengths}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{\LaTeX{} counters}

Each \LaTeX{} counter \meta{name} has a corresponding \TeX{} counter
register (defined internally with \cs{newcount}) with the name
\cs{c@\meta{name}}. All counter assignments are global.



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newcounter
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcounter} \Arg{name} \oarg{within}
  \end{syntax}
  Allocates a new \LaTeX{} counter \meta{name}, initialized to zero,
  together with \cs{the\meta{name}} (defined as
  \cs{arabic}\Arg{name}) and an empty \cs{p@\meta{name}} used as a
  prefix by \cs{ref}. Gives an error if the counter already exists. If
  \meta{within} is given, \meta{name} is reset to zero whenever
  \meta{within} is stepped by \cs{stepcounter} or
  \cs{refstepcounter}. Unlike \cs{counterwithin}, this doesn't change
  \cs{the\meta{name}}. Counters are always global.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{cleanthesis}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \setcounter,
    \addtocounter,
    \stepcounter
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setcounter} \Arg{name} \Arg{integer}
    \cs{addtocounter} \Arg{name} \Arg{integer}
    \cs{stepcounter} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Set the counter \meta{name} to \meta{integer}, add \meta{integer}
  to it, or increment it by one. \cs{stepcounter} also resets all
  counters declared to be reset within \meta{name} (via the optional
  argument of \cs{newcounter} or \cs{counterwithin}). \meta{integer}
  can be anything \TeX{} accepts as a number, e.g., \cs{value}\Arg{other}.
  An undefined counter gives an error. The name \texttt{*} denotes the
  current counter, i.e., the one stored in \cs{@currentcounter}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[setcounter]{adjcalc, assoccnt, caption\_2010-01-09,
  caption\_2011-11-10, cleanthesis, dcounter, frontespizio, locality,
  lwarp, reledmac, xcntperchap}
\modifiedby[addtocounter]{acmart, adjcalc, aguplus, assoccnt,
  caption\_2010-01-09, caption\_2011-11-10, dcounter, floatrow,
  locality, lwarp, reledmac, sublabel}

  caption3\_2007-04-11, caption3\_2010-01-14, caption3\_2011-11-01,
  caption3\_2019-09-01, caption3\_2020-07-29, caption3\_2020-10-26,
  caption\_2019-09-01, caption\_2020-07-29, caption\_2020-10-26,
  datatool-base, floatrow, locality, prosper, reledmac, romanneg,
  scrartcl, scrartcl-xetex-bidi.def, scrbook, scrbook-xetex-bidi.def,
  scrreprt, scrreprt-xetex-bidi.def, sublabel, xassoccnt, xcntperchap,
  zref-perpage}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[user,EXP]
  {
    \value
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{value}\Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Returns the internal counter register \cs{c@\meta{counter}}, so it can
  be used wherever \TeX{} expects a number, e.g., in
  \cs{setcounter}, \cs{ifnum}, or \cs{numexpr}. It does not
  typeset anything; use \cs{the}\cs{value}\Arg{counter} or
  \cs{arabic}\Arg{counter} for that.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{chapterbib, circuitikz-1.7.2-body.tex, crosswrd, currency,
  enumitem, xifthen}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \counterwithin,
    \counterwithout
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{counterwithin} * \oarg{format-cmd} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter}
    \cs{counterwithout} * \oarg{format-cmd} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter}
  \end{syntax}
  The operation that defines that one counter is reset whenever
  another counter is stepped is also available as the command
  \cs{counterwithin}. In contrast to \cs{newcounter}, it alters
  \cs{the\meta{counter}} to typeset
  \cs{the\meta{parent-counter}}\texttt{.}\meta{format-cmd}\texttt{\{\meta{counter}\}}
  where \meta{format-cmd} is a command such as \cs{roman}. If the
  optional argument is not present, it defaults to \cs{arabic}.

  When using the starred form \cs{the\meta{counter}} is not touched,
  which is useful if it needs a more complex definition or is already
  correctly set up. Obviously, in that case the optional argument is
  meaningless and is ignored if given.

  The \cs{counterwithout} command implements the opposite operation;
  without star it sets \cs{the\meta{counter}} to
  \meta{format-cmd}\texttt{\{\meta{counter}\}}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[counterwithin]{chngcntr}
\modifiedby[counterwithout]{chngcntr}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@ifbothcounters
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@ifbothcounters} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Internal helper for \cs{counterwithin} and \cs{counterwithout}:
  executes \meta{code} if both counters exist, otherwise gives an
  error.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{easybase, sjtuarticle, sjtureport, sjtuthesis}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@addtoreset,
    \@removefromreset
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@addtoreset} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter}
    \cs{@removefromreset} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Add \meta{counter} to (or remove it from) the list of counters reset
  when \meta{parent-counter} is stepped. Unlike \cs{counterwithin} and
  \cs{counterwithout} they leave \cs{the\meta{counter}} alone and don't
  check that the counters exist. Widely used in older classes and
  packages; in new code the starred \cs{counterwithin} is preferable.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newcounteralias
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcounteralias} \Arg{alias} \Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{alias} as an alias of the existing \meta{counter}:
  both share the same value, and the representations of \meta{alias}
  (\cs{the\meta{alias}} etc.) use those of \meta{counter}. Useful,
  e.g., for theorem-like environments numbered in one sequence
  but referenced with different names.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{aliascnt}
\publicusedby{keytheorems, pseudo}



\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@stpelt
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@stpelt} \Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Resets \meta{counter} (to $-1$ and then steps it, so that counters
  reset within it are reset as well). Used as \cs{@elt} when
  \cs{stepcounter} processes the reset list.
\end{function}

\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \c@\meta{counter}
  }
  The count register holding the value of the \LaTeX{} counter
  \meta{counter}, allocated by \cs{newcounter} (e.g., \cs{c@page},
  \cs{c@section}). Its value is obtained with \cs{value}\Arg{counter}
  and changed with \cs{setcounter}, \cs{addtocounter}, \cs{stepcounter}
  etc., which also take care of the counters reset by \meta{counter}
  (\cs{cl@\meta{counter}}); assignments to the register directly bypass
  that. \meta{counter} may contain characters other than letters; then the
  command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{function}[settable]
  {
    \the\meta{counter}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{the\meta{counter}}
  \end{syntax}
  The printed representation of \meta{counter}, defined by
  \cs{newcounter} as \cs{@arabic}\cs{c@\meta{counter}}; classes and
  packages redefine it (e.g., \cs{thesection}, \cs{thepage}). Used by
  \cs{ref} (via \cs{@currentlabel}, together with \cs{p@\meta{counter}})
  and wherever the number is typeset. \meta{counter} may contain
  characters other than letters; then the command can only be used via
  \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef},
  \ldots).
\end{function}



\begin{variable}[settable]
  {
    \p@\meta{counter}
  }
  A prefix put in front of \cs{the\meta{counter}} when
  \cs{refstepcounter} sets \cs{@currentlabel}, i.e., when the counter is
  referenced with \cs{ref}. Empty by default; classes set, e.g.,
  \cs{p@enumii} to \cs{theenumi}, so that a reference to an item of a
  nested list shows both numbers. \meta{counter} may contain characters
  other than letters; then the command can only be used via \cs{csname}
  \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \cl@\meta{counter}
  }
  The reset list of \meta{counter}: an \cs{@elt} list
  (\cs{@elt}\Arg{counter_1}\cs{@elt}\Arg{counter_2}\ldots) of the
  counters that are reset to zero when \meta{counter} is stepped with
  \cs{stepcounter} or \cs{refstepcounter}. Extended by \cs{@addtoreset}
  and \cs{counterwithin}, reduced by \cs{counterwithout}. \meta{counter}
  may contain characters other than letters; then the command can only
  be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse},
  \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{function}[settable]
  {
    \theH\meta{counter}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{theH\meta{counter}}
  \end{syntax}
  A representation of \meta{counter} that is unique in the document,
  used to build hyperlink targets: \cs{refstepcounter} sets
  \cs{@currentHref} to \meta{counter}\texttt{.}\cs{theH\meta{counter}}.
  \cs{newcounter} defines it as the arabic value, prefixed with
  \cs{theH}\meta{parent}\texttt{.} if the counter is reset by another
  counter (\cs{@addtoreset}). Packages redefine it if the value of
  \meta{counter} can repeat (e.g., for counters that are reset
  independently of the counters they are numbered within).
  \meta{counter} may contain characters other than letters; then the
  command can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}



\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \alias@ctr@\meta{counter}
  }
  Defined for a counter made an alias of another one with
  \cs{newcounteralias}\Arg{counter}\Arg{other}: holds the name of the
  counter \meta{other} that \meta{counter} shares its value,
  \cs{the\meta{counter}}, \cs{p@\meta{counter}} and reset list with.
  Alias counters cannot be used in \cs{@addtoreset}; the underlying
  counter is found by following these definitions. \meta{counter} may
  contain characters other than letters; then the command can only be
  used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse},
  \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Representation of counter values}

\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \Alph,
    \Roman,
    \alph,
    \arabic,
    \fnsymbol,
    \roman
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{arabic} \Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Typeset the value of \meta{counter} as an arabic number, as a lower
  or uppercase letter (values 1--26 only), as a lower or uppercase
  roman numeral, or as a footnote symbol (values 1--9: $*$, $\dagger$,
  $\ddagger$, \S, \P, $\|$, and doubled versions of the first three). Values
  out of range give an error. They are used in
  definitions of \cs{the\meta{counter}}. The counter name \texttt{*}
  refers to the current counter.
\end{function}
