\sourcefile{ltcounts}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@slowromancap
  }
%
  Macro used in the implementation of \cs{@Roman} to capitalize the
  result in an expandable way.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{amsart, amsbook, amsproc, smfart, smfbook}
\usedby{adigraph, cnltx-base, lectures, njurepo, pageslts, relatese,
  romanbar, srbtiks, xtuformat}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@\meta{style},
    \\meta{style}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@\meta{style}} \meta{count register}
    \cs{\meta{style}} \Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  The counter representations: \meta{style} is one of \texttt{arabic},
  \texttt{roman}, \texttt{Roman}, \texttt{alph}, \texttt{Alph} and
  \texttt{fnsymbol}. \cs{@\meta{style}} takes a count register (or
  number), \cs{\meta{style}} the name of a \LaTeX{} counter.
  \cs{pagenumbering} \Arg{style} sets \cs{thepage} to
  \cs{@\meta{style}}\cs{c@page}, so a package can add a style by
  defining both commands for a new \meta{style}. \meta{style} may
  contain characters other than letters; then the commands can only be
  used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse},
  \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{\LaTeX{} lengths}

\LaTeX{} doesn't distinguishes between skips (variabl lengths) and
dimens (fixed lengths), the high-level user commands only provide
skips (called \enquote{lengths} in the \LaTeX{} manual.



\sourcefile{ltlength}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newlength
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newlength} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Allocates a new skip register as \meta{cmd}, initialized to
  \texttt{0pt}. Gives an error if \meta{cmd} is already defined.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltlength}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \setlength,
    \addtolength
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setlength} \meta{cmd} \Arg{length}
    \cs{addtolength} \meta{cmd} \Arg{length}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the length register \meta{cmd} to \meta{length}, or adds
  \meta{length} to it. \meta{cmd} can be any \TeX{} skip or dimen
  register (or parameter such as \cs{parindent}). \meta{length} may
  include stretch and shrink components, e.g., \texttt{6pt plus 2pt},
  but only if \meta{cmd} is a skip; for a dimen the \texttt{plus}
  part would end up being typeset. The assignment is
  local, unlike counter assignments.

  With the \pkg{calc} package, \meta{length} can be an arithmetic expression.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[setlength]{adjcalc, adjustbox, combinedgraphics, linguho,
  lwarp, realboxes}
\modifiedby[addtolength]{adjcalc, lwarp}



\sourcefile{ltlength}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \settowidth,
    \settoheight
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{settowidth} \meta{cmd} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  Typesets \meta{material} in LR-mode in a temporary box (with
  tagging suspended) and sets the length register \meta{cmd} to the
  natural width (respectively height) of the result. The material is
  not output. \cs{settodepth} is the analogue for the depth.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[settowidth]{linguho}
\modifiedby[settoheight]{olabels}



\sourcefile{ltlength}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@settodim
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@settodim} \meta{box dimension} \meta{register} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  The common implementation of \cs{settowidth} and friends: typesets
  \meta{material} in a temporary box and assigns its
  \meta{box dimension} (\cs{wd}, \cs{ht}, or \cs{dp}) to
  \meta{register}. Normally the user-level commands are preferable.

\end{function}
\modifiedby{chronos}
\publicusedby{}



\sourcefile{ltlength}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@settopoint
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@settopoint} \meta{skip or dimen register}
  \end{syntax}
   This macro takes the contents of the skip or dimen register that is
   supplied as its argument and removes the fractional part to make
   it a whole number of points. This can be used in class files to
   avoid values like |345.4666666pt| when calculating a dimension.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

%===============================================
\section{Hooks, sockets and templates}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{General hook interface}

It is a bit of a debate which hook commands are user facing. Most are
really meant for packages or classes.  A few are sometimes useful in
the preamble or even in the document body and those have been marked
\enquote{user} but this is at best a rough indication. For details see
the documentation of \texttt{lthooks}.



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewHook,
    \NewReversedHook,
    \NewMirroredHookPair
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewHook} \Arg{hook}
    \cs{NewReversedHook} \Arg{hook}
    \cs{NewMirroredHookPair} \Arg{hook\textsubscript1} \Arg{hook\textsubscript2}
  \end{syntax}
  Declare a new hook, i.e., a named place in the code (executed with
  \cs{UseHook}) to which packages and users can add code with
  \cs{AddToHook}. In a reversed hook the code chunks are executed in
  reverse order, which is useful for \enquote{end} hooks matching a
  \enquote{begin} hook; \cs{NewMirroredHookPair} declares such a pair.
  In package code \meta{hook} can start with \texttt{.}, which is
  replaced by the package name. Hook names must be unique and
  declarations are global.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[NewHook]{}
\modifiedby[NewReversedHook]{}
\modifiedby[NewMirroredHookPair]{}
\publicusedby[NewHook]{csvsimple-l3, easybase, fcolumn-2026-01-16,
  hgbthesis, huaz, hyperref, incgraph, jsmembertable,
  latex-lab-testphase-bookmark, memoir, postnotes, robust-externalize,
  scrartcl, scrbook, scrreprt, sjtu-lang-de.def, sjtu-lang-en.def,
  sjtu-lang-ja.def, sjtu-lang-zh.def, sjtu-thesis-preset-base.def,
  tikzducks, tikzlings, tikzlings-anteaters, tikzlings-apes,
  tikzlings-bats, tikzlings-bears, tikzlings-bees, tikzlings-bugs,

  tikzlings-elephants, tikzlings-hippos, tikzlings-koalas,
  tikzlings-marmots, tikzlings-meerkats, tikzlings-mice,
  tikzlings-moles, tikzlings-owls, tikzlings-pandas, tikzlings-penguins,
  tikzlings-pigs, tikzlings-rhinos, tikzlings-sheep, tikzlings-sloths,
  tikzlings-snowmen, tikzlings-squirrels, tikzlings-turkeys,
  tikzlings-wolves, zref-clever}
\publicusedby[NewReversedHook]{}
\publicusedby[NewMirroredHookPair]{fancyhdr, flowfram}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewHookWithArguments,
    \NewReversedHookWithArguments,
    \NewMirroredHookPairWithArguments
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewHookWithArguments} \Arg{hook} \Arg{number}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{NewHook} and friends but the hook takes \meta{number}
  arguments (1--9). They have to be provided by
  \cs{UseHookWithArguments} and can be accessed as \texttt{\#1},
  \ldots{} in code added with \cs{AddToHookWithArguments}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[NewHookWithArguments]{}
\modifiedby[NewReversedHookWithArguments]{}
\modifiedby[NewMirroredHookPairWithArguments]{}
\publicusedby[NewHookWithArguments]{easybase, fcolumn-2026-01-16,
  fcolumn-2026-05-27, spbmark}
\publicusedby[NewReversedHookWithArguments]{}
\publicusedby[NewMirroredHookPairWithArguments]{}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \AddToHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AddToHook} \Arg{hook} \oarg{label} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds \meta{code} to \meta{hook} under the name \meta{label}
  (default: the current package name, or \texttt{top-level} in the
  document). Code with different labels can be ordered with
  \cs{DeclareHookRule}. The hook need not exist yet; generic hooks
  such as \texttt{env/\meta{env}/begin}, \texttt{cmd/\meta{cmd}/before}, or
  \texttt{file/\meta{file}/after} are created on the fly. A \texttt{\#}
  in \meta{code} must be doubled if the hook takes arguments; use
  \cs{AddToHookWithArguments} in that case. Additions are global.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \AddToHookNext
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AddToHookNext} \Arg{hook} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds \meta{code} to the next execution of \meta{hook} only; it is
  executed after the normal hook code and then discarded. Code added
  this way can't be ordered by rules.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \AddToHookWithArguments,
    \AddToHookNextWithArguments
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AddToHookWithArguments} \Arg{hook} \oarg{label} \Arg{code}
    \cs{AddToHookNextWithArguments} \Arg{hook} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Variants of \cs{AddToHook} and \cs{AddToHookNext} for hooks with
  arguments, where \texttt{\#1}, \ldots{} in \meta{code} refer to the
  hook arguments (and a literal \texttt{\#} must be doubled).
\end{function}
\modifiedby[AddToHookWithArguments]{}
\modifiedby[AddToHookNextWithArguments]{}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ActivateGenericHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ActivateGenericHook} \Arg{hook}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{hook} as a generic hook that a package provides
  (executed with \cs{UseHook}) but that is not declared with
  \cs{NewHook}, typically because only some instances of a family
  of hooks are needed. Does nothing if the hook is already activated.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DisableGenericHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DisableGenericHook} \Arg{hook}
  \end{syntax}
  Disables the generic \meta{hook} so that code can no longer be added
  to it (an error is given). Use this, for example, if an environment
  or command implements the hook explicitly and generic hook code
  would never be executed.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{}



\sourcefile{lthooks}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \UseHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseHook} \Arg{hook}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes the code stored in \meta{hook} (in the order determined by
  the hook rules) followed by any \enquote{next} code. Does nothing if
  the hook is empty or undeclared. Package code should normally use it
  only for hooks it has declared itself.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\begin{function}[deprecated]
  {
    \@\meta{name}hook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@\meta{name}hook}
  \end{syntax}
%
  The legacy \LaTeXe{} way of providing hooks: a macro to which code
  is added (e.g., with \cs{g@addto@macro}) and that is executed at the
  right place. These hooks have been (largely) removed from the kernel
  code even if the hook macro itself is still defined to receive code.
  

  When the hook \meta{name} is declared or used by the hook management,
  the code collected in a command \cs{@\meta{name}hook} is moved into
  the hook (as the label \texttt{legacy}) and the command is cleared.
  Remaining commands of that form are typically deprecated; use
  \cs{AddToHook} instead. \meta{name} may contain characters other than
  letters; then the command can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{}
  \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}

\subsection{Sockets and plugs}

Sockets are named places in the code whose behavior is determined by
an assigned \enquote{plug}, so that different implementations (e.g.,
with and without tagging) can be switched in and out. For details see
the documentation of \texttt{ltsockets}.



\sourcefile{ltsockets}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewSocket
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewSocket} \Arg{socket} \Arg{number of inputs}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a new socket that expects \meta{number of inputs}
  arguments. It automatically gets a plug \texttt{noop}, which
  removes the inputs; sockets with one input also get the plug
  \texttt{identity} (returning the input unchanged), which is then
  the default. Only allowed at top level, not in a group.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{gia-handout, hyperref, sillypage}



\sourcefile{ltsockets}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \UseSocket
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseSocket} \Arg{socket} \meta{inputs}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes the plug currently assigned to \meta{socket}, passing it
  the \meta{inputs} (as many brace groups as declared). For
  performance reasons there is no check that the socket exists.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{cuted, hyperref}



\sourcefile{ltsockets}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewSocketPlug
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewSocketPlug}  \Arg{socket}  \Arg{plug} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{plug} for \meta{socket}: \meta{code} is executed when
  the plug is assigned and the socket is used, with the socket inputs
  available as \texttt{\#1}, \texttt{\#2}, \ldots. Gives an error if
  the plug already exists. The declaration is local.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{asmeconf, asmejour, footmisc, gia-handout, hyperref,
  l3backend-pdf-luatex.def, l3backend-testphase-luatex.def, ltx-talk,
  moloch-talk, sblarticle, sblbook, sblreport, scrartcl, scrbook,
  scrreprt, sillypage}

  if either doesn't exist. The assignment is local.
\end{function}

\subsection{Templates and instances}

Most of the code for templates is written in the L3 programming layer
and is internal, i.e., the commands start with \texttt{\_\_}. Here we only
describe the public functions. For details see the documentation of
\texttt{lttemplates}.



A \emph{template type} describes an abstract design object (e.g.,
\enquote{sectioning}) and the number of arguments it takes; a
\emph{template} implements a type with a set of keys; an
\emph{instance} is a template with concrete key values that can be
used in code.



Despite the fact that template declarations have CamelCase names we do
not list them as user facing because they are mainly intended for
programmers defining design solutions. Typically used either in the
\LaTeX{} kernel or in class or package files.



%...............................................
\subsubsection{Declaring templates}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewTemplateType
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewTemplateType} \Arg{type} \Arg{\# of arguments}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a new template \meta{type}; every template and instance of
  this type takes \meta{\# of arguments} arguments when used.
  A template type can only be declared once!
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{diffcoeff, hustthesis, ltx-talk, sjtuthesis, sysuthesis,
  talkthemespectrum, xfrac}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateInterface
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateInterface} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{\# of arguments} \Arg{key spec}
  \end{syntax}
  Declare the interface for a template named \meta{name} of type
  \meta{type}. The \meta{\# of arguments} must match the number
  declared for \meta{type}.
%
  The \meta{key spec} specifies all keys understood by the template,
  their key-type and if applicable, a default value for each, in the
  form \meta{key}\texttt{\,:\,}\meta{key type}\texttt{\,=\,}\meta{default}.

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{acro2, diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, easybase, enotez,
  exsheets\_headings.def, fduthesis, fduthesis-en, hustthesis, ltx-talk,
  moloch-talk, njuthesis, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis, sjtuthesis,
  substances, sysuthesis, talkthemespectrum, talkthemetcolorbox,
  tamu-talk-header, tamu-talk-titlepage, tasks, xfrac}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \KeyValue
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \meta{key2} : \meta{key type} = \cs{KeyValue} \Arg{key1}
  \end{syntax}
  Refers to the value of another key of the same template. Can be
  used as default values for keys, so that one key follows another
  unless set explicitly. Can also be used in \cs{DeclareInstance} or
  \cs{EditInstance} to specify key values there.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \EditTemplateDefaults
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{EditTemplateDefaults} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{new defaults}
  \end{syntax}
  Replaces the defaults of template \meta{name} by the key--value list
  \meta{new defaults}. This affects instances declared afterwards;
  existing instances are unchanged.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, talkthemetcolorbox, xfrac}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateInterfaceEquivalents
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateInterfaceEquivalents} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \oarg{date} \Arg{key spec}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares additional keys for template \meta{name} that act as
  equivalents of its base keys, e.g., as an alias or as a key that sets
  several base keys. If \meta{date} is given, the keys are
  deprecated from that date and their use produces a warning. Useful
  for renaming keys without breaking existing instances.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateCode
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateCode} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{\# of arguments} \Arg{key bindings} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Implements template \meta{name}: \meta{key bindings} maps each key
  of the interface to a variable (e.g.,
  \texttt{indent = \textbackslash l\_mytemplate\_indent\_dim}), and
  \meta{code} is executed when the template is used, with the
  arguments of the type as \texttt{\#1}, \ldots. Key values are
  assigned to the variables before \meta{code} (or at
  \cs{AssignTemplateKeys}).

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{acro2, diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, easybase, enotez,
  exsheets\_headings.def, fduthesis, fduthesis-en, hustthesis, ltx-talk,
  lwarp-enotez, moloch-talk, njuthesis, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis,
  sjtuthesis, substances, sysuthesis, talkthemespectrum,
  talkthemetcolorbox, tamu-talk-header, tamu-talk-titlepage, tasks,
  xfrac}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \AssignTemplateKeys
  }
  Used directly (not nested in a macro) inside the \meta{code} of
  \cs{DeclareTemplateCode} to delay the assignment of the key values
  to their variables until this point; otherwise they are assigned
  before \meta{code} starts.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\publicusedby{acro2, diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, easybase, enotez,
  exsheets\_headings.def, fduthesis, fduthesis-en, hustthesis,
  lwarp-enotez, njuthesis, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis, sjtuthesis,
  substances, sysuthesis, tasks}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \SetTemplateKeys,
    \SetKnownTemplateKeys
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{SetTemplateKeys} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Used inside the \meta{code} of \cs{DeclareTemplateCode} to
  override key values, typically with a key--value list passed by
  the user as an argument. \cs{SetTemplateKeys} gives an error for
  unknown keys, \cs{SetKnownTemplateKeys} stores them in
  \cs{UnusedTemplateKeys}. If used together with
  \cs{AssignTemplateKeys} the latter should come first.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateCopy
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateCopy} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{from-name}
  \end{syntax}
  Copies the template definition with the name \meta{from-name} to the
  template with name \meta{name}.
%
  Afterwards one can alter defaults or the code implementation. In

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}

\subsubsection{Declaring template instances}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareInstance
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareInstance} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{template} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares instance \meta{name} of \meta{type} using \meta{template},
  with the template's defaults modified by \meta{key settings}.

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \EditInstance
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{EditInstance} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Edits some or all of the key settings for the existing instance
  \meta{name} of type \meta{type}.

  Does not change the used template. If that is necessary then
  \cs{DeclareInstance} has to be used to overwrite the existing
  declaration.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareInstanceCopy
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareInstanceCopy} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{from-name}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares instance \meta{name} of \meta{type} to be a copy of the
  existing instance \meta{from-name} (of the same type).

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\subsubsection{Showing template and instance information}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ShowTemplateInterface,
    \ShowTemplateDefaults,
    \ShowTemplateVariables,
    \ShowTemplateCode
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ShowTemplateInterface} \Arg{type}  \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  For the template \meta{name} of type \meta{type} the commands show the
  \begin{description}
  \item[interface] i.e., keys and associated key types
  \item[defaults] i.e., default values for the keys (if any)
  \item[variables] i.e., key bindings to variables used in code
  \item[code] i.e., the code that implements the template functionality
  \end{description}

  The display is implemented with an \cs{errmessage} so \TeX{} stops
  its processing to allow inspection.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[ShowTemplateInterface]{}
\modifiedby[ShowTemplateDefaults]{}
\modifiedby[ShowTemplateVariables]{}
\modifiedby[ShowTemplateCode]{}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ShowInstanceValues
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ShowInstanceValues} \Arg{type} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  For the instance \meta{name} of type \meta{type} all keys and their
  current values are displayed. The template that was used for the
  instance is given as a pseudo key called \verb*=from template=.


  The display is implemented with an \cs{errmessage} so \TeX{} stops
  its processing to allow inspection.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{lttemplates}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DebugTemplatesOn,
    \DebugTemplatesOff
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DebugTemplatesOn} ... \cs{DebugTemplatesOff}
  \end{syntax}
  Turn on (or off) debugging information about the use of templates
  and instances, i.e., messages at the point where they are used
  (which are normally suppressed for performance reasons).
\end{function}
\modifiedby[DebugTemplatesOn]{}
\modifiedby[DebugTemplatesOff]{}

\section{Messages, errors and debugging}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Package and class messages}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \PackageError
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{PackageError}\Arg{package}\Arg{message}\Arg{help message}
  \end{syntax}
  Generates an error message for package \meta{package} displaying
  \meta{message} on the terminal introduced by \texttt{Package
    \meta{package} Error:}.  Processing is stopped and awaits a
  reaction from the user. If the user replies with pressing \texttt{h}
  the \meta{help message} is shown as well.

  Inside \meta{message} the command \cs{MessageBreak} can be used to
  produce suitable line breaks to structure the message.  Displaying
  and formatting the error message is done using \cs{GenericError}
  internally.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \PackageWarning,
    \PackageWarningNoLine,
    \PackageNote,
    \PackageNoteNoLine,
    \PackageInfo,
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{PackageWarning}\Arg{package}\Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Generates a package warning on the terminal (with or without
  displaying the current line number). The \meta{message} is preceded
  by \texttt{Package \meta{package} Warning:}. The command
  \cs{MessageBreak} can be used to produce suitable line breaks to
  structure the message.  Displaying and formatting the warning
  message is done using \cs{GenericWarning} internally.

  The commands \cs{PackageNote} and \cs{PackageNoteNoLine} only differ
  in that they use \texttt{Package \meta{package} Info:} at the
  beginning, i.e., they show their \meta{message} on the terminal but
  not as a warning; instead they offer \enquote{information} of some
  kind.

  The command \cs{PackageInfo} is like \cs{PackageNote} but writes its
  \meta{message} only to the transcript and not to the terminal.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[PackageWarning]{gmbase, letterspace, msg, olabels, silence,
  skeyval-ltxcmds.tex}
\modifiedby[PackageWarningNoLine]{silence, skeyval-ltxcmds.tex,
  tudscrartcl, tudscrbook, tudscrposter, tudscrreprt}
\modifiedby[PackageNote]{}
\modifiedby[PackageNoteNoLine]{}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \MessageBreak
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{PackageWarning}\Arg{package}\{\meta{text}\cs{MessageBreak}\meta{more text}\}
  \end{syntax}
  Starts a new line inside the message of \cs{PackageError},
  \cs{PackageWarning}, etc., indented and prefixed so that it lines up
  with the first line (e.g., with \texttt{(\meta{package})}). Outside
  such messages it is \cs{relax}.
\end{function}

\subsection{Generic and kernel messages, standard errors}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@nocounterr
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@nocounterr} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Issues the error \enquote{No counter '\meta{name}' defined}. Use it
  in code that tests for counters, e.g., in the false branch of
  \cs{@ifundefined}\texttt{\{c@\meta{name}\}}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \GenericError
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{GenericError} \Arg{continuation} \Arg{message} \Arg{explanation} \Arg{help}
  \end{syntax}
  The basis for all \LaTeX{} error messages. Displays \meta{message}
  (where \cs{MessageBreak} starts a new line beginning with
  \meta{continuation}) followed by \meta{explanation} (e.g., a
  reference to the documentation) and stops; \meta{help} is shown if
  the user types \texttt{h}. In packages and classes use
  \cs{PackageError} or \cs{ClassError} instead.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{bxcoloremoji, hyperref, pdfnotiz, silence,
  skeyval-ltxcmds.tex, srdp-tables, tabu}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \GenericInfo,
    \GenericWarning
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{GenericInfo}\Arg{continuation}\Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  The basis for all \LaTeX{} warnings and info messages, with
  \meta{continuation} used after each \cs{MessageBreak}.
  \cs{GenericWarning} writes to the terminal and the transcript file,
  \cs{GenericInfo} only to the latter.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@latex@error,
    \@latex@warning,
    \@latex@warning@no@line,
    \@latex@note,
    \@latex@note@no@line
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@latex@error} \Arg{message} \Arg{help text}
    \cs{@latex@warning} \Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Error, warning or info messages for use in the \LaTeX{} kernel. They
  announce themselves as \texttt{LaTeX Error:}, \texttt{LaTeX Warning:},
  or \texttt{LaTeX Info:}.

  They should normally only be used by the kernel, i.e., not in
  package or classes. There, one should use \cs{PackageError},
  \cs{ClassWarning}, etc.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[int,deprecated]
  {
    \@latexbug
  }
  %
  This command generates an error that claims that there may be a bug
  in \LaTeX{} itself. While that is quite possible it is something
  that should not be claimed in any package or class code. Thus this
  command \textbf{should not be used} anywhere and eventually it will
  get also removed from the two places it is still used in the kernel
  (because it is essentially nonsense there).

\end{function}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@eha,
    \@ehb,
    \@ehc,
    \@ehd
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@latex@error}\{Unknown symbol font `\#2'\}\cs{@eha}
  \end{syntax}
  Simple fixed help texts for error messages used together with
  \cs{@latex@error} as shown in the example.

  \cs{@eha} gives \texttt{Your command was ignored. Type ...}

  \cs{@ehb} gives \texttt{You've lost some text. \cs{@ehc}}

  \cs{@ehc} gives \texttt{Try typing <return> to proceed. If that doesn't
  work ...}

  \cs{@ehd} gives the lovely \texttt{You're in trouble here. \cs{@ehc}}
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  { \@badend,
    \@badlinearg,
    \@badmath,
    \@badpoptabs,
    \@badtab,
    \@ctrerr,
    \@fltovf,
    \@nocnterr,
    \@nodocument,
    \@noitemerr,
    \@nolnerr,
    \@notdefinable,
    \@notprerr,
    \@parmoderr,
    \@toodeep,
    \@LRmoderr
  }
%
  Commands that expand to \cs{@latex@error} with a
  fixed \meta{message} and one of the \cs{@eha}, \cs{@ehb}, or
  \cs{@ehd} help texts, e.g., \cs{@badend} produces the error message
  \begin{quote}\ttfamily
    \meta{env} on line \meta{number} ended by \meta{other env}
  \end{quote}

  Only a few \LaTeX{} errors have such extra commands (usually those
  from the days of \LaTeX\,2.09). Most of the time \cs{@latex@error} is
  used directly in the code.

\end{function}

\subsection{Tracing and debugging}

\sourcefile{lterror}
\begin{variable}[user,settable]
  {
    \c@errorcontextlines
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setcounter}\texttt{\{errorcontextlines\}\{100\}}
  \end{syntax}
  \LaTeX{} counter that defines how many lines from the macro
  processing stack are shown when an error occurs. Default value is
  \texttt{-1} as they are usually not helpful for most users. But if
  one needs to see the context it can be useful to set it to a high
  enough number.

  This is the \LaTeX{} name for the engine primitive \cs{errorcontextlines}.
\end{variable}
\setby{dtk, moredefs, texpower, tikz-kalender}



\begin{variable}[int,settable]
  {
    \errorcontextlines
  }
  The \TeX{} integer parameter behind the \LaTeX{} counter
  \texttt{errorcontextlines}; set it through \cs{setcounter}.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{variable}

  etex, fcltxdoc, gmRCS, gmampulex, gmbase, gmcommand, gmdoc, gmdocc,

\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \tracingfonts
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{tracingfonts}\texttt{=}\meta{number}
  \end{syntax}
  Controls the amount of tracing information about font selection
  written to the log (0: none, up to 4: everything including math
  font setup).

  Needs \pkg{tracefnt} package.

  This is not the engine primitive \cs{tracingfonts} but a \LaTeX{} command
  replacing it; the original primitive is still available as
  \cs{tex_tracingfonts:D} but not to be used.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@pkg-disable@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@pkg-disable@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}}
  \end{syntax}
  Defined by \cs{disable@package@load}\Arg{file}\Arg{code}: a later
  request to load the package \meta{file} executes \meta{code} instead
  and issues an info message. Removed by \cs{reenable@package@load}.
  The name contains characters other than letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}

\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \opt@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  }
  The comma separated list of options the package or class
  \meta{file}.\meta{ext} was loaded with (also those given with
  \cs{PassOptionsToPackage}); tested by \cs{@ifpackagewith} and
  \cs{@ifclasswith}. The name contains characters other than letters, so the
  command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \@raw@opt@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  }
  The options of the package or class \meta{file}.\meta{ext} as
  given, i.e., without the normalization done for
  \cs{opt@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}}
  (spaces in \texttt{key=value} options are kept); used by the
  key-value option processing. The name contains characters other than
  letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \ds@\meta{option}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ds@\meta{option}}
  \end{syntax}
  The code declared with \cs{DeclareOption}\Arg{option}\Arg{code},
  executed by \cs{ProcessOptions} if \meta{option} was given. \meta{option}
  may contain characters other than letters (e.g., \texttt{11pt}); then the
  command can only be used via \cs{csname}
  \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \unprocessedoptions-\meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{unprocessedoptions-\meta{file}.\meta{ext}}
  \end{syntax}
  Set while loading the package or class \meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  (to \cs{@@unprocessedoptions}): if the package doesn't process its
  options (\cs{ProcessOptions}, \cs{ProcessKeyOptions}), it is executed
  at the end of the package and reports the options as unused.
  Undefined again afterwards. The name contains characters other than
  letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Options: key-value interface}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \opt@handler@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{opt@handler@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}}
  \end{syntax}
  The key-value option handler of the package or class
  \meta{file}.\meta{ext}, set up by \cs{ProcessKeyOptions}; used to
  process options passed later, e.g., by a second \cs{usepackage} with
  options. The name contains characters other than letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Checking what is loaded}



\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \ver@\meta{file}.\meta{ext}
  }
%
  Defined when the package or class \meta{file}.\meta{ext} is loaded
  (\meta{ext} is \texttt{sty} or \texttt{cls}): holds the date, version
  and description given in its \cs{ProvidesPackage} or
  \cs{ProvidesClass} declaration (or is empty). \cs{@ifpackageloaded},
  \cs{@ifpackagelater} and their class versions test it. The name
  contains characters other than letters, so the command can only be
  used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse},
  \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Preamble-only commands and deferred code}

\sourcefile{ltdefns}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@onlypreamble
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@onlypreamble}\meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds \meta{cmd} to the list of commands that are disabled at
  \cs{begin}\texttt{\{document\}}: afterwards using \meta{cmd} gives
  the error \enquote{Can be used only in preamble}. Use it for
  declarations that only make sense in the preamble.
\end{function}

\subsection{Rollback for packages and classes}

\sourcefile{ltclass}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareRelease,
    \DeclareCurrentRelease
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareRelease} \Arg{name} \Arg{date} \Arg{file}
    \cs{DeclareCurrentRelease} \Arg{name} \Arg{date}
  \end{syntax}
  Used at the top of a package or class to support rollback: each
  \cs{DeclareRelease} names an older release (\meta{name} may be
  empty), the date from which it applies, and the \meta{file}
  containing it (by convention
  \meta{package}\texttt{-}\meta{date}\texttt{.sty}).
  \cs{DeclareCurrentRelease} declares the current release and must come
  last. If a rollback date or name is requested (via the optional
  date argument of \cs{usepackage} or via \pkg{latexrelease}), the
  matching file is loaded instead.
\end{function}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Kernel rollback}

\sourcefile{ltvers}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \EndIncludeInRelease
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{IncludeInRelease}\Arg{date}\meta{cmd}\Arg{description}
    \ \ \meta{code}
    \cs{EndIncludeInRelease}
  \end{syntax}
  Ends a code block started with \cs{IncludeInRelease}. Such blocks
  are used in the kernel (and in packages) for rollback support: when
  an older format date is requested only the blocks whose \meta{date} is
  not later than the requested date are executed. For each \meta{cmd}
  the blocks are given newest first and the last one has date
  \texttt{0000/00/00}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{contract}
\publicusedby{fontaxes, scrbase, scrbase-20260202}



\sourcefile{ltvers}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewModuleRelease,
    \EndModuleRelease
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewModuleRelease}\Arg{date}\Arg{name}\Arg{description}
    \ \ \meta{code}
    \cs{IncludeInRelease}\texttt{\{0000/00/00\}}\Arg{name}\Arg{description}
    \ \ \meta{undo code}
    \cs{EndModuleRelease}
  \end{syntax}
  Marks a whole new module of code (e.g., a new kernel file). When
  rolling back to a date before \meta{date} the module is skipped and
  only the \meta{undo code} is executed (which, e.g., undefines
  commands of the module).
\end{function}
\modifiedby[NewModuleRelease]{}
\modifiedby[EndModuleRelease]{}
\publicusedby[NewModuleRelease]{}
\publicusedby[EndModuleRelease]{}

\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \@file-subst@\meta{file}
  }
  Defined by \cs{declare@file@substitution}\Arg{file}\Arg{subst}:

\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \cp@\meta{file}
  }
  The checkpoint of the \cs{include} file \meta{file}: the values of all
  counters at its end, written to the \texttt{.aux} file
  (\cs{@writeckpt}) and read back with \cs{@setckpt}, so the counters
  are correct after an \cs{include} file that is not read because of
  \cs{includeonly}. \meta{file} may contain characters other than letters;
  then the command can only be used via
  \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef},
  \ldots).
\end{variable}

\subsection{Writing files}

\sourcefile{ltclass}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \filecontents,
    \endfilecontents
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{filecontents}\oarg{options}\Arg{filename}
    \ \  ...
    \cs{end}\Arg{filecontents}
  \end{syntax}
  Writes the environment body verbatim to \meta{filename}. By default
  an existing file is not overwritten (use the \texttt{overwrite}
  option) and a header comment is added (suppress with
  \texttt{noheader}); \texttt{nosearch} only checks the current
  directory. The star form \env{filecontents*} never adds a
  header. Can be used anywhere, also before \cs{documentclass}.
\end{function}

  engines more read streams), so they are a limited resource.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \openin,
    \openout
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{openin} \meta{stream} \texttt{=} \meta{file}
    \cs{immediate}\cs{openout} \meta{stream} \texttt{=} \meta{file}
  \end{syntax}
  Open \meta{file} for reading or writing on
  \meta{stream}. Without \cs{immediate}, \cs{openout} is delayed until
  the page is shipped out. Close with \cs{closein} or \cs{closeout}.

  These are engine primitives.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \read
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{read} \meta{stream} \texttt{to} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Reads the next line (or more, if braces are
  unbalanced) from \meta{stream} and defines \meta{cmd} locally with
  it. Stream numbers outside 0--15 read from the terminal. See also
  \cs{readline} (e-\TeX{}).

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \wlog,
    \protected@wlog
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{wlog} \Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Writes \meta{message} to the transcript file on a line by
  itself. Commands inside \meta{message} are expanded, which may
  result in errors depending on the content. \cs{protected@wlog} is
  like \cs{wlog} but sets \cs{protect} in a suitable way so that
  robust commands behave as in \cs{typeout}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \message
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{message} \Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Writes \meta{message} to the terminal and

  one can use \texttt{\textasciicircum\textasciicircum J}. The
  \meta{message} is expanded. In \LaTeX{} code \cs{typeout} is
  usually preferable.

  This is an engine primitive.
\end{function}

%===============================================
\section{Characters, encodings and symbols}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Declaring encoding-specific commands}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd},
    \?\\meta{cmd},
    \\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd}-\meta{char},
    \\meta{enc}-cmd
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd}}
    \cs{?\\meta{cmd}}
    \cs{\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd}-\meta{char}}
    \cs{\meta{enc}-cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  The definitions behind an encoding-specific command \cs{\meta{cmd}}:
  \cs{\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd}} is its definition in encoding \meta{enc} (made by
  \cs{DeclareTextCommand}, \cs{DeclareTextSymbol}, \ldots),
  \cs{?\\meta{cmd}} the default used in encodings without own definition
  (\cs{DeclareTextCommandDefault} etc.), and
  \cs{\meta{enc}\\meta{cmd}-\meta{char}} a composite of \cs{\meta{cmd}} with the
  character or command \meta{char} (\cs{DeclareTextComposite}).
  \cs{\meta{enc}-cmd} is set to \cs{@changed@cmd} for every encoding
  declared with \cs{DeclareFontEncoding}; it handles commands without
  a definition for \meta{enc} by installing the default
  \cs{?\\meta{cmd}} (or an error if there is none). The names contain
  a backslash (and other non-letters), so they can't even be generated
  with \cs{csname} directly; use \cs{expandafter}\cs{string} or the
  declaration commands.
\end{function}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Accents}

\sourcefile{ltoutenc}
\begin{function}[user,EXP]
  {
    \",
    \',
    \.,
    \~,
    \b,
    \c,
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{"}\meta{base letter}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  These commands typeset various diacritics. These days \LaTeX{} is
  fully Unicode-aware (even in 8-bit engines like \pdfTeX{}) so that
  one normally simply writes \texttt{ä} instead of \cs{"}\texttt{a} (or even
  \cs{"}\texttt{\{a\}} as it was recommended in Lamport's manual).

  However, this remains a valid input syntax and it makes it possible
  to even produce glyphs not part of Unicode, e.g., \"\$ (produced
  with \cs{"}\cs{\$}). If the current font encoding has a precomposed
  glyph it is used, otherwise the accent is placed over the base
  letter.

\end{function}

\subsection{Text symbols}

These days characters and symbols can be entered directly as UTF-8
encoded characters (and typeset if the used font supports them). Many
of them are also available via command names, largely for historical
reasons, when \TeX{} was still 8-bit based. In certain situations these
are still useful, for example, if your keyboard doesn't allow you
easily to produce a certain Unicode character.



There are also a few that need command names because they serve as
syntax characters in \TeX{}.



%\begin{function}[]

%

\typeout{The command \string\% fails in function and in \string\cs }



\sourcefile{ltoutenc,ltplain}
\begin{function}[user,EXP]
  {
    \$,
    \#,
    \&,
    \textasciitilde
  }
%
  They produce \$, \#, \&; using them directly as characters is not
  easily possible as they have syntax functions. For
  \textasciitilde\ one needs to use the long command name, because
  \cs{~} is used for a tilde accent.

  There is also \cs{\%} for a percent sign (without the backslash it
  would start a line comment). Due to some limitation of the macros we
  use here it can't be displayed in the syntax box.

\end{function}

\subsection{Superscripts and subscripts in text}

\sourcefile{ltfloat}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \textsuperscript,
    \textsubscript
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{textsuperscript} \Arg{text}
    \cs{textsubscript} \Arg{text}
  \end{syntax}
  Typesets \meta{text} raised (lowered) in the script size of the
  current font, e.g., for ordinals or chemical formulas in text. The
  work is done by \cs{@textsuperscript} and \cs{@textsubscript}.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltfloat}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@textsuperscript,
    \@textsubscript
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@textsuperscript} \Arg{text}
  \end{syntax}
  Implementation of \cs{textsuperscript} and \cs{textsubscript}: set
  \meta{text} in the script size (\cs{sf@size}) and raise or lower it
  by \cs{textsuperscript@offset} or \cs{textsubscript@offset},
  followed by \cs{textsuperscript@space} or \cs{textsubscript@space}.
  Also used for the footnote marks (\cs{@makefnmark}).

  This is no longer using math mode to raise the characters, as that
  would result in badly tagged documents announcing a formula when
  there is none (or only for layout purposes).
\end{function}

  {
    \textsuperscript@offset,
    \textsubscript@offset
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{textsuperscript@offset}
    \cs{textsubscript@offset}
  \end{syntax}
  Dimen expressions giving the amount by which \cs{textsuperscript}
  raises and \cs{textsubscript} lowers its material (in box 0 when
  evaluated). By default computed from the font parameters of the math
  fonts (the \cs{Umath\ldots} parameters in Lua\TeX), so the result
  matches that of math mode.
\end{function}

\section{Fonts (NFSS)}

In NFSS a font is described by five attributes: encoding, family,
series, shape, and size. For details see \texttt{fntguide}.

\subsection{Document-level font commands}

\sourcefile{ltfntcmd}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \emph,
    \strongemph
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{emph}  \Arg{text}
    \cs{strongemph}  \Arg{text}
  \end{syntax}
  Mark \meta{text} as emphasized text or strongly emphasized
  text. Rendering depends on configuration. \cs{emph} usually
  alternates between italics and normal shape, \cs{strongemph}
  typically uses bold face. Configurable through declarations
  \cs{DeclareEmphSequence} and \cs{DeclareStrongEmphSequence}.
  The corresponding declarations are \cs{em} and \cs{strongem}.
\end{function}

\modifiedby[strongemph]{}



\sourcefile{ltfssini}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareEmphSequence,
    \DeclareStrongEmphSequence
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareEmphSequence} \Arg{list of font changes}
  \end{syntax}
  The \meta{list of font changes} is a comma separated list whose
  entries are used when \cs{emph} is called (later entries are used if
  \cs{emph} is nested). An entry is skipped if it doesn't change the
  current font (unless it contains \cs{emforce}). If the nesting is
  deeper than available entries \cs{emreset} is used after the last
  entry and then the sequence is repeated. The declarations are
  additive, e.g.,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{DeclareEmphSequence}\{\cs{itshape},\cs{upshape}\cs{scshape},\cs{itshape}\}
  \end{alltt}

  \cs{DeclareStrongEmphSequence} provides the same for \cs{strongemph}.

\end{function}
\modifiedby[DeclareEmphSequence]{}
\modifiedby[DeclareStrongEmphSequence]{}
\publicusedby[DeclareEmphSequence]{fduthesis, fontspec-luatex,
  fontspec-xetex, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis, rwth-fonts}
\publicusedby[DeclareStrongEmphSequence]{}

\sourcefile{ltfssini}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \emforce,
    \strongemforce
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareEmphSequence}\{\cs{itshape},\cs{color}\{red\}\cs{emforce}\}
  \end{syntax}
  Used inside an entry of \cs{DeclareEmphSequence}
  (respectively \cs{DeclareStrongEmphSequence}) to force the use of
  that entry even if it doesn't change the font, e.g., if it only
  changes the color.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltfssaxes}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \itshape,
    \normalshape,
    \scshape,
    \slshape,
    \sscshape,
    \swshape,
    \ulcshape,
    \upshape
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \Arg{\cs{itshape} \meta{text}}
  \end{syntax}
  Declarations selecting the italic, normal (\cs{shapedefault}),
  small caps, slanted, spaced small caps, swash, upper/lowercase, or
  upright shape. They combine with the current shape where it makes
  sense, e.g., \cs{itshape} after \cs{scshape} gives italic small
  caps if available. Commands with argument are \cs{textit} etc.
\end{function}

\subsection{Selecting fonts}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \curr@fontshape
  }
  A shorthand for
  \cs{f@encoding}\texttt{/}\cs{f@family}\texttt{/}\cs{f@series}\texttt{/}\cs{f@shape},
  i.e., the current font shape without the size.
\end{variable}
\modifiedby{mlltxchg.def}

  ctex-engine-luatex.def, everysel-2011-10-28, figureversions,

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \wrong@fontshape
  }
  Internal helper used during font selection when the requested shape
  is not available: it determines a substitute (first changing the
  shape, then the series, then the family to the encoding defaults),
  records the substitution, and warns.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{ltxtools-trace, nfssext-cfr-nnfss}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@defaultsubs
  }
  Internal macro that is either empty or contains a warning message
  displayed at the end of the run that some font substitutions have
  happened during the run.

  Currently used in some places outside of the kernel (but only
  because the classes overwrite core \LaTeX{} commands rather than
  using hooks!)
\end{function}
\modifiedby{pseudo}
\usedby{aastex701, combine, ltxutil, revtex4, revtex4-1, revtex4-2}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontencoding
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontencoding} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the encoding attribute for the next \cs{selectfont}. The
  encoding must have been declared (normally by loading \pkg{fontenc}).
\end{function}
\modifiedby{huaz, hyperref, mltex, ucshyper, wordcount.tex, zugferd}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontfamily
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontfamily} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the family attribute, e.g., \texttt{cmr} or \texttt{lmss},
  for the next \cs{selectfont}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{huaz, hyperref, wordcount.tex, zugferd}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontsize
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontsize} \Arg{size} \Arg{baselineskip}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the size attribute and the \cs{baselineskip} (multiplied by
  \cs{baselinestretch}) for the next \cs{selectfont}. Without unit,
  \texttt{pt} is assumed. Document-level size commands like
  \cs{small} are defined with it.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{huaz, hyperref, wordcount.tex, zugferd}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \linespread
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{linespread} \Arg{factor}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets \cs{baselinestretch} to \meta{factor}, i.e., scales the
  \cs{baselineskip} of all font sizes, taking effect at the next
  \cs{selectfont}. Typically used in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{wordcount.tex}

    \usefont

  did not change).

  {

  }

  \cs{baselineskip} used by the last \cs{fontsize} or
  \cs{linespread}.

\sourcefile{ltfssbas,ltfssaxes}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontseries,
    \fontseriesforce
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontseries} \Arg{series}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the series attribute for the next \cs{selectfont}. The
  requested \meta{series} is combined with the current one according
  to the rules declared with \cs{DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule}; the
  \texttt{force} variant sets \meta{series} without consulting
  the rules.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[fontseries]{huaz, hyperref, wordcount.tex, zugferd}
\modifiedby[fontseriesforce]{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas,ltfssaxes}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontshape,
    \fontshapeforce
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontshape} \Arg{shape}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the shape attribute for the next \cs{selectfont}, combined
  with the current shape according to the rules declared with
  \cs{DeclareFontShapeChangeRule}; the \texttt{force} variant
  bypasses the rules.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[fontshape]{huaz, hyperref, wordcount.tex, zugferd}
\modifiedby[fontshapeforce]{}



\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \selectfont
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontfamily}\Arg{family}\cs{fontseries}\Arg{series}\cs{selectfont}
  \end{syntax}
  Selects the font described by the current attributes (as set by
  \cs{fontencoding}, \cs{fontfamily}, \cs{fontseries},
  \cs{fontshape}, and \cs{fontsize}), loading it if necessary, and
  sets up the baselineskip and math fonts accordingly.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{CJK, enumitem, everysel-2011-10-28, huaz, hyperref,
  ltxtools-trace, nolbreaks, pxeverysel, quantumarticle, quantumview,
  standalone, truncate, ucshyper, wordcount.tex, ximera, xjyutping,
  zugferd}




%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Font declarations}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontShape
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontShape} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size specs} \Arg{special}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares which external fonts to use for the given combination of
  attributes at which sizes. \meta{size specs} is a list of entries
  such as \texttt{<10> cmr10} or \texttt{<->s*[0.95] fontname},
  possibly using size functions like \texttt{sub} or \texttt{ssub}
  for substitutions. \meta{special} is code executed each time the
  font is loaded (often empty). Usually found in \texttt{.fd} files;
  the \meta{family} must have been declared with \cs{DeclareFontFamily}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFixedFont
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFixedFont} \meta{cmd} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} as a fast switch to one fixed font, bypassing
  the NFSS selection mechanism. Useful for fonts used often in a fixed
  size (e.g., in headers); \meta{cmd} doesn't update
  \cs{baselineskip}, math fonts, or the current font attributes.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{fix-tudscrfonts}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontFamily
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontFamily} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{special}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{family} in \meta{encoding}. The \meta{special} code
  is executed when any font of the family is loaded, typically to set
  \cs{hyphenchar} or \cs{skewchar}. Usually the first declaration in
  an \texttt{.fd} file.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{ctex-engine-pdftex.def}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontFamilySubstitution
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontFamilySubstitution} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{substitution}
  \end{syntax}
  Attempts to load \texttt{.fd} files for \meta{family} and the
  \meta{substitution} family in \meta{encoding} if not loaded already
  and then substitutes all kind of standard shapes from the
  \meta{substitution} family to \meta{family}. This means that from
  that point onwards a request for a shape in \meta{family} will
  always use the shape from \meta{substitution}.

  The substitution is done with \texttt{ssub}, i.e., silently and only
  recorded in the \texttt{.log} file.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \DeclareErrorFont
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareErrorFont} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size}
  \end{syntax}
  For a fully functional NFSS setup there has to be one
  \cs{DeclareErrorFont} declaration for each \meta{encoding} known to
  NFSS. Its purpose is to select this font shape when a requested font
  shape can't be found and the automatic substitution
  mechanism also doesn't lead to an existing font.

  This declaration should only be used by the kernel or by the few
  packages that provide additional \meta{encoding}s for \LaTeX. It
  \emph{should not} be used by packages that provide additional fonts,
  which is why it is marked as internal in this document!

  Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{bxjsarticle, bxjsbook, bxjsreport, bxjsslide}
\usedby{arabic.ldf, eu1enc.def, eu2enc.def, farsi.ldf, laeenc.def,
  lfeenc.def, lgienc.def, ly1enc.def, mlltxchg.def}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontEncoding
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontEncoding} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{text settings} \Arg{math settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a new font encoding. \meta{text settings} is executed each
  time the encoding is selected in text, \meta{math settings} when it
  is used for a math alphabet. The commands for the encoding-specific
  glyphs are declared separately (e.g., in an \texttt{\meta{enc}enc.def}
  file) and loaded with \pkg{fontenc}. Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontSubstitution
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontSubstitution} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the default font shape for \meta{encoding} that is used as the
  last resort when automatic font substitution doesn't find the
  requested shape. These fonts must exist (at least in one size),
  which is checked at \cs{begin}\texttt{\{document\}}. Only available
  in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontEncodingDefaults
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontEncodingDefaults} \Arg{text settings} \Arg{math settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares code executed for every encoding in addition to the
  encoding's own settings (stored in \cs{default@T} and
  \cs{default@M}). Use \cs{relax} for an argument that should not
  be changed. Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareEncodingSubset
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareEncodingSubset} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{subset}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares that \meta{family} supports only a subset of
  \meta{encoding} (currently only used for \texttt{TS1}).
  \meta{subset} ranges from \texttt{0} (all glyphs available) to
  \texttt{9} (many missing). A \meta{family} ending in \texttt{-*}
  covers the common variants such as \texttt{-LF} and
  \texttt{-OsF}. Usually placed in \texttt{.fd} files.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{nfssext-cfr}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \CheckEncodingSubset
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{CheckEncodingSubset} \meta{use cmd} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{fallback} \Arg{subset} \meta{symbol}
  \end{syntax}
  Used in definitions of text symbols: if the current family supports
  \meta{symbol} (i.e., its declared subset of \meta{encoding} is
  lower than \meta{subset}), executes \meta{use cmd}
  (\cs{UseTextSymbol} or \cs{UseTextAccent})\Arg{encoding}\meta{symbol};
  otherwise \meta{fallback}\meta{symbol}, e.g., an error or a faked
  glyph. See \texttt{lttextcomp.dtx} for examples.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclarePreloadSizes

  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclarePreloadSizes} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size list}
  \end{syntax}
  Loads the given font shape in the sizes of the comma separated
  \meta{size list} already at format generation or in the preamble.
  Rarely needed these days. Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}

\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \cdp@list
  }
  Holds the declared encodings with their substitution
  defaults as a list of
  \cs{cdp@elt}\Arg{encoding}\Arg{family}\Arg{series}\Arg{shape}
  entries. It is built by \cs{DeclareFontEncoding} and
  \cs{DeclareFontSubstitution} and used to check the defaults at
  \cs{begin}\texttt{\{document\}} and whether an encoding has been
  declared. Only available in the preamble.
\end{variable}

\subsection{Font axes and change rules}

\sourcefile{ltfssaxes}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule,
    \DeclareFontShapeChangeRule
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule} \Arg{current} \Arg{request} \Arg{result} \Arg{alternative}
  \end{syntax}
  Define how \cs{fontseries} (or \cs{fontshape}) combines the
  \meta{current} value with a \meta{request}, e.g., that requesting
  \texttt{b} while the current series is \texttt{c} (condensed) gives
  \texttt{bc}. If \meta{result} doesn't exist in the font family,
  \meta{alternative} is tried; if neither exists or there is no rule,
  \meta{request} is used. Mainly for font support packages.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule]{}
\modifiedby[DeclareFontShapeChangeRule]{}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{constant}
  {
    \@vpt,
    \@vipt,
    \@viipt,
    \@viiipt,
    \@ixpt,
    \@xpt,
    \@xipt,
    \@xiipt,
    \@xivpt,
    \@xviipt,
    \@xxpt,
    \@xxvpt
  }
  Shorthands for typical font sizes for use in places where fonts are
  selected, e.g., in class files in \cs{fontsize}\cs{@xpt}\cs{@xiipt}.
  Default values are \texttt{5}, \texttt{6}, \texttt{7},
  \texttt{8}, \texttt{9}, \texttt{10}, \texttt{10.95}, \texttt{12},
  \texttt{14.4}, \texttt{17.28}, \texttt{20.74}, and \texttt{24.88}.
\end{constant}

\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \set@fontsize
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{set@fontsize} \Arg{linespread factor} \Arg{font size} \Arg{baselineskip}
  \end{syntax}
  The internal form of \cs{fontsize} with an explicit factor for the
  baselineskip. Classes and packages call it rather than \cs{fontsize}
  when the factor should not be \cs{baselinestretch}.
  \meta{font size} and \meta{baselineskip} can be given without a unit
  in which case \texttt{pt} is assumed.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{jlreq, microtype, stfloats}
\publicusedby{CJK, bxjsarticle, bxjsbook, bxjsreport, bxjsslide,
  everysel-2011-10-28, interfaces-LaTeX, ltxtools-trace, relsize,
  setspaceenhanced, typehtml, xepersian}



\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \size@update,
    \glb@settings
  }
  Helper macros for font handling: \cs{size@update} applies a pending
  size change (baselineskip, strut) at \cs{selectfont}, and
  \cs{glb@settings} sets up the math fonts for a new size.

  Supposed to be internal but is used by quite a number of
  packages. Such overwrite of core internals are really very
  questionable.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[size@update]{bxjsarticle, bxjsbook, bxjsreport, bxjsslide,
  jlreq, stfloats}
\modifiedby[glb@settings]{}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareSizeFunction
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareSizeFunction} \Arg{name} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a font size function named \meta{name} for use in the size
  specifications of \cs{DeclareFontShape}. The \meta{code} sets
  \cs{external@font} based on the requested size and the arguments
  of the function.

  Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{typeface}
\publicusedby{CJK, kotexutf, lucenc.def, semhelv, semlcmss,
  sjtu-math-font-stixtwo.def}



\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \execute@size@function
  }
  Executes the size function found in a \cs{DeclareFontShape}
  specification.

  This isn't meant to be changed (but some classes do---check why,
  perhaps there is a hook missing).
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltfsstrc}
\begin{variable}[settable]
  {
    \fontsubfuzz,
    \font@submax
  }
  %
  \cs{font@submax} is highest amount of font size adjustments that
  happened due to font substitutions so far. At the end of the run
  this value will be reported if it exceeds \cs{fontsubfuzz}.

  Both are implemented as macros and not as \TeX{} registers (to save
  on registers which was a problem in the early days of \LaTeXe{}).
\end{variable}
\setby[fontsubfuzz]{IEEEtran, anyfontsize, easybase}
\setby[font@submax]{anyfontsize}
\publicusedby[fontsubfuzz]{aastex701, combine, ltxutil, revtex4,
  revtex4-1, revtex4-2}
\publicusedby[font@submax]{aastex701, combine, ltxutil, revtex4,
  revtex4-1, revtex4-2}

\subsection{Math font declarations}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareMathSizes
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareMathSizes} * \Arg{text size} \Arg{math text size} \Arg{script size} \Arg{scriptscript size}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares the sizes of the math fonts to be used when the text font
  has \meta{text size}. If \meta{math text size} is empty, no math
  fonts are set up for that size (useful for large headings). The
  star form only declares the sizes if none were declared before. For
  sizes without declaration, the sizes are computed with
  \cs{defaultscriptratio} and \cs{defaultscriptscriptratio}. Only
  available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \ifmath@fonts,
    \math@fontsfalse,
    \math@fontstrue
  }
  Switch that decides whether math fonts are set up for the current
  size (false for sizes declared without math sizes).

  Only used in kernel + ams. Replace?
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \calculate@math@sizes
  }
  Computes the math sizes for the current text size from
  \cs{defaultscriptratio} and \cs{defaultscriptscriptratio} if no
  \cs{DeclareMathSizes} declaration exists for it (and gives an info
  message).
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

  unicode-math-xetex}



\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{variable}[settable]
  {
    \defaultscriptratio,
    \defaultscriptscriptratio
  }

  Ratios used when calculating math sizes for a given text size, i.e.,
  no \cs{DeclareMathSizes} is given. Defaults are \texttt{.7} and

\begin{constant}[]
  {
    \sym\meta{name}
  }
  The math group number of the symbol font \meta{name} declared with
  \cs{DeclareSymbolFont} (e.g., \cs{symletters}, \cs{symoperators});
  used in \cs{DeclareMathSymbol}, \cs{DeclareMathDelimiter} etc. and in
  \cs{mathcode} and \cs{fam} assignments. \meta{name} may contain
  characters other than letters; then the command can only be used via
  \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef},
  \ldots).
\end{constant}



\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \mv@\meta{version},
    \mv@\meta{version}@frozen,
    \mv@\meta{version}@reset,
    \c@mv@\meta{version}
  }
  The data of the math version \meta{version}: \cs{mv@\meta{version}}
  holds the code setting up the math groups of the version (built by
  \cs{DeclareMathVersion}, \cs{SetSymbolFont},
  \cs{DeclareMathAlphabet}, \ldots), executed by \cs{glb@settings},
  i.e., in the first formula after a change of size or math version;
  the count register \cs{c@mv@\meta{version}} holds the number of
  allocated math groups.

  Math alphabets used for the first time are allocated on the fly. In
  the preamble this is permanent; in the document the version is
  \enquote{frozen} as soon as only \cs{c@localmathalphabets} math groups
  are left: \cs{mv@\meta{version}@frozen} becomes a copy of
  \cs{mv@\meta{version}}, the count is saved and
  \cs{mv@\meta{version}@reset} is defined. From then on further
  allocations are local to a formula: \cs{mv@\meta{version}@reset}
  (empty until the version is frozen) is executed after every formula
  (\cs{check@mathfonts} adds it with \cs{aftergroup}) and, at the top
  math level, undoes the allocations beyond the frozen state;
  \cs{mathversion}, used inside a top-level formula, resets a frozen
  version unconditionally. \meta{version} may contain characters other
  than letters; then the commands can only be used via \cs{csname}
  \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{function}[int,readonly]
  {
    \S@\meta{size}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{S@\meta{size}}
  \end{syntax}
  The math font sizes for text size \meta{size} (in points, without
  unit): sets \cs{tf@size}, \cs{sf@size} and \cs{ssf@size} as declared
  with \cs{DeclareMathSizes} or computed on first use. The name contains
  characters other than letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{function}

  Code to apply after the next \cs{selectfont}, used by
  \cs{fontsize} to defer adjustments. Normally empty.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}
\usedby{}



\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \\meta{enc}/\meta{family}/\meta{series}/\meta{shape},
    \\meta{enc}/\meta{family}/\meta{series}/\meta{shape}/\meta{size}
  }
  The first one holds the font shape data declared by
  \cs{DeclareFontShape} for the shape (sizes and fonts to use), the
  second is the font identifier of a loaded font, i.e., a command
  defined with \cs{font}, e.g., \texttt{\textbackslash T1/cmr/m/n/10}.
  \cs{selectfont} defines the latter from the former. The name contains
  characters other than letters, so the command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \\meta{enc}+\meta{family}
  }
  Defined (as \cs{@empty}) when NFSS has tried to load the font
  definition file \meta{enc}\meta{family}\texttt{.fd}, so the file is
  read only once. The name contains characters other than letters, so the
  command
  can only be used via \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or
  \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef}, \ldots).
\end{variable}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \T@\meta{enc},
    \M@\meta{enc},
    \D@\meta{enc}
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{T@\meta{enc}}
    \cs{M@\meta{enc}}
    \cs{D@\meta{enc}}
  \end{syntax}
  The settings of the font encoding \meta{enc}: \cs{T@\meta{enc}} is the
  text code and \cs{M@\meta{enc}} the math code from
  \cs{DeclareFontEncoding} (executed when the encoding is selected in
  text or math), \cs{D@\meta{enc}} sets the default family, series and
  shape from \cs{DeclareFontSubstitution}. \cs{T@\meta{enc}} is also
  tested to find out whether an encoding is declared. \meta{enc} may contain
  characters other than letters (digits count as such, e.g., \texttt{T1});
  then the command can only be used via
  \cs{csname} \ldots{} \cs{endcsname} (or \cs{@nameuse}, \cs{@namedef},
  \ldots).
\end{function}

\section{Spacing, line and page breaking}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Spaces and skips}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ 
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{\space} \cs{\space} \cs{\space}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  The command \verb*=\ = typesets a space character, same as just
  using a \verb*= =, but it can be used in places where a normal space
  gets ignored, e.g., after a command such as \verb*=\LaTeX\ =. Several
  such commands in a row produce multiple spaces in contrast to using
  several normal spaces in a row, e.g., the example above would produce 3
  spaces.

  The \verb*=\ = command is a \TeX{} primitive for typesetting a space
  and for some operations, such as assigning a \cs{catcode} to the
  space character or displaying a space in \cs{typeout} one needs to
  use \cs{\space} to refer to this character.

  The command \cs{space} is a command that contains a space character
  as its replacement material. For typesetting this is identical to
  using \verb*=\ = but in other cases there are differences:
  \cs{csname}\texttt{ X}\cs{space}\cs{endcsname} produces a macro name with
  a space
  character in the name. In that position \cs{\space} (as a
  typesetting instruction) would not be allowed. For the same reason
  you need to use \cs{space} and not \cs{\space} inside \cs{typeout}.

\end{function}



\sourcefile{ltplain}
\begin{constant}[user]
  {
    \space
  }
  Expands to a space character. See \cs{\space} above for the
  differences between the two.
\end{constant}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \addvspace
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{addvspace} \Arg{skip}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds vertical space of \meta{skip}, but if the preceding item was
  also space added by \cs{addvspace}, only the larger of the two is
  used (so that, e.g., consecutive lists or headings don't accumulate
  space). Must be used in vertical mode; in a paragraph it ends the
  paragraph first, but in an \cs{hbox} it gives an error. Used by
  lists and sectioning commands.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{adfathesis, bxcalcize, classicthesis, lhelp, ndsu-thesis,
  ndsu-thesis-2022, rhode-island-thesis, tocbasic, toptesi, tvz-hax,

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \vspace,
    \hspace
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{vspace} * \Arg{skip}
    \cs{hspace} * \Arg{skip}
  \end{syntax}
  Add vertical or horizontal space of \meta{skip}, which may contain
  stretch and shrink (and \pkg{calc} expressions). Space added at a
  page or line break is normally discarded; the star forms keep it.
  \cs{vspace} in a paragraph adds the space after the current line.
\end{function}

\subsection{Line and page breaks}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \pagebreak,
    \nopagebreak
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{pagebreak} \oarg{number}
  \end{syntax}
  Encourage (respectively discourage) a page break at this point,
  with strength \meta{number} from \texttt{0} (slight) to \texttt{4}
  (forced, or prohibited); default is \texttt{4}. In a paragraph, the
  break applies after the current line.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \linebreak,
    \nolinebreak
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{linebreak} \oarg{number}
  \end{syntax}
  Encourage (respectively discourage) a line break at this point in a
  paragraph, with strength \meta{number} from \texttt{0} to
  \texttt{4} (default). Unlike \cs{newline}, a line ended with
  \cs{linebreak} is still justified.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \samepage
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \Arg{\cs{samepage} \meta{material}}
  \end{syntax}
  Discourages page breaks within \meta{material} by setting various
  penalties to 10000 (within the current group). Breaks between
  paragraphs remain possible; it is rarely effective, so
  \cs{nopagebreak} or a \env{minipage} is often a better choice.
\end{function}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \addpenalty
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{addpenalty} \Arg{penalty}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds a \meta{penalty} in vertical mode in front of the preceding
  space (added by \cs{addvspace}), so that a page break at that point
  removes the space. Does nothing if \cs{if@nobreak} is true or in a
  minipage. Used, e.g., before headings.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{tocbasic}



\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \nobreakdashes
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{nobreakdashes}\texttt{--}
  \end{syntax}
  Placed directly before a hyphen or dash, prevents a line break after
  it (e.g., in \texttt{1}\cs{nobreakdashes}\texttt{--3}), while still
  allowing hyphenation of the following word. Use it only in front of
  \texttt{-}, \texttt{--}, or \texttt{---}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{}

  class.
\end{variable}

\subsection{Hyphenation}

\sourcefile{ltfssbas}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \showhyphens
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{showhyphens} \Arg{words}
  \end{syntax}
  Shows all hyphenation points of \meta{words} on the terminal and in
  the log, indicated by \texttt{-} in the output. It does this by
  deliberately generating an underfull box, so the output appears as a
  box warning. Uses the hyphenation rules of the current language.
\end{function}
\modifiedby{lwarp-xltxtra, microtype-luatex.def, microtype-pdftex.def}

\sourcefile{ltspace}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@bsphack,
    \@esphack
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@bsphack} \meta{material} \cs{@esphack}
  \end{syntax}
  Used around commands that produce no visible output (e.g.,
  \cs{label}, \cs{index}, \cs{marginpar}) so that they don't add extra
  space: if there was a space before \cs{@bsphack}, the space after
  \cs{@esphack} is ignored. Only active in horizontal mode.
\end{function}

\section{Mathematics}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsection{Math environments and equation numbering}

\sourcefile{ltmath}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \(,
    \)
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{(} \meta{inline math} \cs{)}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  \LaTeX's alternative to \verb=$...$= for inline formulas. \cs{(}
  gives an error if already in math mode and \cs{)} if not, so
  mismatched delimiters are detected, but many authors prefer
  \verb=$...$= as it is easier to read in the source.
\end{function}



\sourcefile{ltmath}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \[,
    \]
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{[} \meta{display math} \cs{]}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  \LaTeX's short commands for unnumbered display formulas, same as the
  \env{displaymath} environment. It is not equivalent to the plain
  \TeX{} syntax \verb=$$...$$=, which does not work correctly with
  several \LaTeX{} features (e.g., \texttt{fleqn}, tagging) and should
  not be used in a \LaTeX{} document!
\end{function}



\sourcefile{ltmath}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \math,
    \endmath
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{math}  \meta{inline math} \cs{end}\Arg{math}
  \end{syntax}
  Long environment form of \cs{(}\ldots\cs{)}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[math]{envmath, lwarp, nath, nfssfox.tex}
\modifiedby[endmath]{alatex, breqn, breqn-xetex-bidi.def,
  breqn-xetex-xepersian.def, envmath, lwarp, nath}

    \displaymath,
    \enddisplaymath
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{displaymath}  \meta{display math} \cs{end}\Arg{displaymath}
  \end{syntax}
  Long environment form of \cs{[}\ldots\cs{]}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[displaymath]{envmath, lwarp, onlyamsmath, standalone}
\modifiedby[enddisplaymath]{envmath, lwarp, standalone}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@kernel@eqno,
    \@kernel@leqno
  }
  %
  Saved version of the \TeX{} primitives \cs{eqno} and \cs{leqno}
  which are then redefined by \LaTeX{}. They are not supposed to be
  used directly.

  \cs{@kernel@eqno} is the \LaTeX{} name for the engine primitive \cs{eqno}.
  \cs{@kernel@leqno} is the \LaTeX{} name for the engine primitive \cs{leqno}.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[@kernel@eqno]{}
\modifiedby[@kernel@leqno]{}
\usedby[@kernel@eqno]{}
\usedby[@kernel@leqno]{}



\sourcefile{ltmath}
\begin{function}[]
  {
    \eqno,
    \leqno
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{eqno} \meta{equation number material}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  These are not the \TeX{} primitives to add an equation number to a
  displayed equation, but are redefined by \LaTeX{} to do more work
  (ignoring spaces after the number) and only then internally call the
  \TeX{} primitives (which have been renamed to \cs{@kernel@eqno} and
  \cs{@kernel@leqno}). In documents use \env{equation} instead.

  This is not the engine primitive \cs{eqno} but a \LaTeX{} command
  replacing it; the original primitive is still available as
  \cs{@kernel@eqno} but not to be used.
  This is not the engine primitive \cs{leqno} but a \LaTeX{} command
  replacing it; the original primitive is still available as
  \cs{@kernel@leqno} but not to be used.
\end{function}
\modifiedby[eqno]{IEEEtran, IEEEtrantools, amsart, amsbook, amsproc,
  amsthm, latex-xetex-bidi.def, mathpartir, nath, plain-xetex-bidi.def}
\modifiedby[leqno]{IEEEtran, IEEEtrantools, amsart, amsbook, amsproc,

\sourcefile{ltmath}
\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \cos,

    \cosh,

    \csc,
    \max,

  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{lim}\_\Arg{x \cs{to} \cs{infty}}

  \cs{mathrm}-like style) with proper spacing as a math operator. Some
  of them (\cs{lim}, \cs{limsup}, \cs{liminf}, \cs{max}, \cs{min})
  place sub- and superscripts below and above in display style. New
  operators can be defined with \cs{DeclareMathOperator} from
  \pkg{amsmath}.
